president. - the next item is the report (a4-0173/97) by mr de gucht, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy, on the proposal from the commission to the council (com (97) 0173 - c4-0173/97). centralism means that arrogant administrators think they know everything better than the people who experience the regional problems and who themselves choose solutions for them. moreover, if the vernacular is not the language of education, government and the economy, a division arises between first-class citizens who have grown up with the dominant language at home and second-class citizens who have only learned it. there can be no democratic governance in europe without taking into account cultural diversity and regional differences. the existence of the european union leads to an increase in the power of the governments of the member states vis-à-vis their national parliaments and their regions. this increase in scale is at the expense of the positions which scotland, catalonia, friesland, corsica, flanders and the aosta valley have now acquired, whereas it is precisely in these regions that the desire for greater assimilation to the member states is felt. the napolitano report, which protects regional and local authorities from large-scale centralistic thinking and action, is therefore an indispensable contribution to democracy and peaceful coexistence in europe.
the napolitano report on the role of local and regional authorities in european integration is an important step for me, as a former local government official, to get europe back on its feet. the european union's officials and politicians are too often sitting in the cathedrals of supranational power and forget that europe really consists of four levels of government: the european union is a global community of nations. europe's roots lie at the local and regional level. the european lives and works there, and most of the policies we make in europe are implemented there. the napolitano report recognizes the importance of the local and regional entity for the survival and deepening of european integration. and not just the formal regions with constitutional powers, but all the regions. from dutch provinces, english counties to german länder, spanish autonomous communities. in a europe where all citizens are equal and therefore have equal rights, it is not possible to distinguish between territorial entities and to give more rights to one region than to another. it is true, of course, that each member state has the right to determine its own constitutional arrangements, and that means that decentralisation is regulated differently in one country than in another. i think that mr napolitano has made some very good proposals to involve regional and local every day. i hope that this report will lead to the convention actually bringing europe and the region closer to the citizens and that we will firmly anchor the region in a new european constitution.
the annual report on human rights in the european union is a source of much disagreement and confusion every year. there are two problems with this. firstly, it is not easy for any member of this parliament who has been elected on a national list and who would like to be re-elected to agree to criticism of his own country. to be able to really put one's hand in one's own bosom, one must somewhat detach oneself from national and party political loyalties, and that is sometimes too much to ask. secondly, until recently it was unclear what human rights these reports should actually be about. what is the measuring plate or the frame of reference? in the past, various rapporteurs have made their own selection of the issues and this has not always been conducive to continuity and credibility. it was therefore a good decision on the part of the commission, which is the principal authority, and of parliament as a whole, to take the community charter of fundamental rights as a basis for these reports. the european parliament's role of control is political and not legal. we must therefore consider the charter as a political reference framework, as a kind of table of contents, for the purpose of these annual reports. this is a chance to check, with this charter in hand, whether the member states are complying with the human rights provisions which are binding and which are contained in numerous conventions of the united nations, the council of europe, the ilo, and so on. human rights are universal, indivisible and interrelated. human rights discourse is by definition global. the european union's human rights policy is therefore only credible if it measures human rights violations at home by the same standards as shortcomings elsewhere in the world. the european parliament is speaking out again at each session on specific human rights problems elsewhere and rightly always attaches great importance to human rights in discussions on the candidate countries. but then we must also be honest with ourselves. that is why i have deliberately chosen the naming and shaming approach in my report. it's not fun, it's fair. the european union is a community of values. that's a pain in the ass. but we must also be prepared to see the serious violations of human rights in one or more member states as a european matter and to ask ourselves what the european union as such can do to improve the situation. the recommendations in my report are therefore addressed not only to one or more or all member states but also, where appropriate, to the commission and the council. i am pleased, as usual, to see commissioner vitorino here again, but i am naturally disappointed that the council is conspicuous by its absence or that some official must have hidden under the sofa. what are the main human rights problems within the european union? i will mention a few of them and ask a number of specific questions. the first is the danger that civil measures against terrorism be identified and evaluated. my question is: the commission and the council are prepared to undertake such an inventory and evaluation? secondly: the misconduct of police and prison staff, which is reported year after year and often falls on the weakest groups, is present in all eu countries, albeit in varying degrees. internal correction mechanisms are not very effective. i believe it is time that this problem was put on the agenda of the european union and that at least a comprehensive investigation into these abuses was carried out. my question is: will i have noted, thanks also to my colleagues in the committee on social affairs, a serious lack of compliance by all the member states with the european social charter, the ilo conventions, etc. it is necessary to clarify how these social obligations under the treaty relate to the obligations of the same member states under secondary community law. my question is: will the commission take the lead in this? finally, i would like to ask the council representative - who is not here, but perhaps the official who is hiding somewhere can pass on this information - what has happened to the decision of the general affairs council in june 2001 to better coordinate internal and external human rights policy. the same question could also be answered by the commission and parliament themselves. if i may, - people and goods travel longer distances these days. far too much of that transport is by road or by air. rail transport is more environmentally friendly, but our rail networks date largely from a time when we were much more confined to state lines than we are today. now almost everyone agrees on modernisation, with trains that can cross the border with the same wagons, the same staff, the same power and the same safety requirements. this can be achieved quickly by enhanced cooperation between national railway companies or by merging large-scale and cross-border activities into one european company. unfortunately, this scaling up is now being misused to force all the member states of the european union to grant access to the rail network to other private-capital companies. liberalisation means that we only drive where the entrepreneurs expect to make a profit. the increasing costs of planning, monitoring, security and infrastructure are going to the government, the taxpayer, and the financial benefits are going to international corporations. the pressure to liberalize will make it more difficult to guarantee continuity and security. despite the continued european unity, in many places there is less cross-border rail traffic today than before the eu. international night trains are being cancelled, long distance services are being cut off, railway books are no longer issued 'abroad', boarding bans are being introduced and no railway facilities are being built for the rapid transport of perishable goods. even before the compromise of the end of 2000 on the designation of corridors for freight traffic by other companies comes into force, attempts are already being made to push through even further liberalisation with the aim of first putting international freight traffic, then domestic freight traffic, then international passenger traffic and finally all transport in the hands of companies with fewer obligations to society as a whole. in the netherlands, which wanted to lead the way, liberalisation has led to a sharp deterioration in the quality of rail services. part of the package of four reports now proposed is detrimental to the railway undertaking's task. if we don't take that part, the future looks a lot better.

in writing. - (nl) safety decisions are usually preceded by fatal accidents. other regulations take precedence until a regulation becomes unavoidable. the question is then one of freedom of enterprise, cost reduction and free competition. it was well known that allowing professional drivers to work too long would lead to accidents. unfortunately, this evidence has never prevented the sector from allowing longer periods of uninterrupted work than in other branches, where the potential damage is less severe. the contractors want to avoid at all costs hiring a second driver or observing waiting times because these measures cost money. in addition, although they too long for protection from overwork and overwork, drivers are eager to return home after a long journey. self-employed drivers even feel they can escape any regulation, and entrepreneurs who want to take advantage of this sell their trucks to their drivers. if we give in to these opposing forces, the right transport companies and the railways will be brought to their knees by competition. for this reason, it is a major step forward that all trucks and courier services operating in the eu - even if they are driven by an independent driver or from outside the eu - comply with the standard of a minimum of 12 hours rest, a daily working time of 9 hours and 90 hours for two weeks.

- mr president, commissioner, 20 years ago aquaculture was touted as the solution to the declining fish stocks. the dream was that this could also provide a significant share of the protein needs of people in the hungry areas of this world. but like many dreams, this one didn't come true. the food conversion rate of farmed fish is low. to produce 1 kilogram of fish, you need not 4 kilograms of feed as in mammals but only 1.5 to 2 kilograms. unfortunately, much of this food must be animal protein. protein in fish feed comes from fishmeal, which in turn comes from industrial fisheries. it's like a nylon stocking that traps entire areas of empty space. it catches not only adult fish but also undersized fish and processes cod blood, among other things. it is therefore pointless to talk about cod recovery plans unless we first put a stop to industrial fishing. this can be done by quotas, but also by forcing fish meal consumers to look for alternative raw materials such as vegetable proteins or zooplankton. i understand that these alternative resources are not readily available. it is therefore of great importance to give financial impetus to the research into these alternatives and to encourage it wherever possible. this has not only served the cod stock in the north sea but also the hungry part of the world's population. if science can tap into these alternative sources of protein for fish feed, the dream of aquaculture will come true.

the rapporteur. - madam president, when we look at the european agricultural policy, two things stand out. firstly, it is well known that it accounts for almost half the budget. secondly, we can that's enough. we have had a new procedure since 1996 which means that we have an annual closure of the accounts and multiannual decisions on the conformity of those accounts, that is to say, on whether that budget has been properly implemented. in 1996 a mediation body was set up to resolve any conflicts between the commission and the member states and the accreditation of the paying - mr. president, aside from sailors and soldiers, in the old days, only the richest and most powerful people traveled far from home. only a small privileged group could buy goods produced far away. today, the economy has expanded enormously, many people work outside their own homes and spend their holidays far from home. raw materials, intermediate products and finished products are moved over great distances from places where production is cheapest to other places where many buyers are expected to pay a high price. the existence of the european union has further reinforced this trend, including the introduction of a common currency, wide freedom for duty-free air traffic and the construction of cross-border motorways. for a long time, the benefits of this scaling up were the only things that were emphasized. it was seen as a great step forward that the transportation needed for this was becoming proportionately cheaper. the opinion leaders preferred not to see that growing traffic flows lead to increasing space consumption, air pollution, noise pollution and road accidents. but more and more people are experiencing the downsides. we now know that it is important to reduce unnecessary transport and to opt for modes of transport that take up less space and pollute the environment less. so it's time to choose. that is also the name of the european commission's white paper on transport until 2010 which we are to consider today. are we really making a choice here? the commission has tried to distinguish at least between the car and the airplane, which are increasingly polluting the environment, and the environmentally friendly transport by rail and water. this involves shifting existing transport flows and channelling any further growth in a way that will reasonably allow people and the environment to survive in an increasingly densely populated area. the first reactions to this from stakeholder organisations and from this parliament were unfortunately negative. no one is against the growth of rail or ship transport, but for air and road transport, they asked for equal treatment, so there is room to grow at least as fast. the european union's policy should therefore be directed towards creating excess capacity at the expense of the taxpayer. this costly overcapacity gives freight hauliers the freedom to choose the mode of transport that is the fastest or cheapest for them at the moment. moreover, such overcapacity may lead to increased competition. this is because workers, especially those in the railways and ports, are less certain of their job and income. they are then played against people in other sectors who are equally insecure about a stable supply of work. all kinds of liberalization proposals can have negative effects on people and their environment. unfortunately, it seems that the choices that are most needed are still not being made to a sufficient extent until 2010. we shall then see railways replaced by motorways in the new member states, a development against which mr piecyk has just warned. it's not the way it should be, and unfortunately, we don't have that kind of guarantee.

firstly, as mr prodi has already said, we must ensure that the economies of the new member states are integrated into those of the present member states. we must promote economic activity and to do this we must first of all ensure better investment opportunities in those countries and we must examine all the instruments to make this possible. the second priority of the budget is to improve the administrative capacity in those countries. how can they manage the enormous sums of money they receive and how can they ensure that good projects are submitted? then a word about the various budget headings. firstly, the first heading on agriculture. everything will depend on the results of commissioner fischler's midterm review, but apart from that we would like to see some attention paid to a number of issues. firstly, the question of the exact relationship between the payment of premiums in agriculture and the environmental directives that europe has. we shall have to determine that more precisely. the second point concerns the possibility of developing insurance schemes for animal diseases in the future. we are currently seeing the bird flu in the netherlands, we have known foot-and-mouth disease, we have known swine fever. we'll have to investigate that. is it possible to take further measures to promote the sale of agricultural products, especially those of high quality? heading 2 is the structural funds. the first thing we must do is to keep our promises. we must ensure that the countries to which the structural funds are allocated receive them and that the administrative constraints are not too restrictive. we will have to examine what the consequences of the n+2 rule are and what the consequences of the 4% performance reserve are. section 3 is devoted to internal policies. some items in this section are always fixed. for what remains, we will have to pay attention to what europe can do in the field of counterterrorism - very topical these days. what can europe do better than the individual member states? what can we do to create an area of freedom, justice and security, to better protect the external borders and to improve the asylum policy? what can we do to improve nuclear safety in the new member states? finally, what can we do about the proliferation of agencies? it seems that every year a number of agencies are added. and finally, what can we do about the ageing of europe? as always, section 4 will require special attention, especially at this time. what are the consequences of a possible crisis in iraq or a crisis in the middle east? we shall again have many points to face and we shall have to keep a close eye on them. heading 5 is administrative expenditure. we will have to look carefully at the results of the reform in the commission. we will also have to see what the results have been of the additional allocation of officials that we have done in the past and so on. the last point, section 7. the copenhagen summit decided that aid to turkey could be included in heading 7, and the commission shares that view. however, the council has also said that we cannot start looking at whether negotiations with turkey can start until 2004. we shall have to see whether the title of this section needs to be changed and whether we should divide it into other sub-sections, and so on. last point, mr president, i hear your hammer. i would like to see good cooperation with everyone in this parliament, especially with the many committees. finally, i shall also pay particular attention to the point raised by mr elles.

in writing. - (nl) the ports between hamburg (germany) and le havre (france), including all dutch and belgian ports, face more competition than all other ports. this is because all these ports serve essentially the same large hinterland including the german ruhr area. this allows cargo flows to be moved continuously from one port to another. in these ports, the transhipment costs per unit of cargo are therefore already significantly lower than the transhipment costs observed in the americas or east asia. it is also in these ports that the influence of the port directive, which is intended to encourage competition and thus reduce the cost of certain port activities, is most radical. these ports cannot work even cheaper and yet they are forced to do so. the risk of social dumping and increased insecurity is therefore much greater than in ports with a de facto monopoly on a smaller hinterland. the port or port state which sets the highest standards of safety, environment, quality of work and working conditions loses out to competition, while the worst performing port wins out. but that's not all! the directive will also force the member states of the european union to breach the commitments they have made under the ilo convention. the adoption at second reading of self-help and the disqualification of certain positions on commitments under the ilo convention is a source of conflict at third reading, with subsequent legal proceedings and other strike actions.
in writing. - (nl) the strikes in ports are due in particular to the section of the proposal for a directive on self-help. this passage also concerns the position of pilots, the duration of concessions, the social conditions of workers and the transparency of state aid, as well as the free development of ports. the common position is not perfect but nevertheless offers an adequate answer with regard to, for example, the time limits for concessions and the free development of ports. progress is also being made in the field of piloting services. the points still under discussion are the state aid directives and the working conditions of dockers, particularly in the light of the provisions on self-help. as regards the first point, parliament's amendments clarify the role of the commission and the time limit set for it. the second point, however, is more complex. self-help, if carried out with too much leeway, risks degenerating into fierce competition, with all the disadvantages that result. unfortunately, the procedure does not allow us to prevent this risk at european level. the national authorities must now do all they can to eliminate distortions of competition in this area. otherwise, the specter of incompetent dockers could well materialize and that is in no one's interest. i accept parliament's position, despite all its (necessary) shortcomings. in accepting this position, i am in any case avoiding giving the council a free hand and i am urging the member states to act. practices, a high basic standard which must be applied throughout europe and in which european rules must not undermine national achievements. information on rights and additional codes of conduct is necessary. point two, the right to information. information on products and on the production process is crucial. of course, not every consumer walks into a manufacturer's shop to inquire about the manufacturing process. research shows that only 10% of consumers are interested, but this 10% is leading and decisive, especially if it is supported by powerful consumer organisations. this 10% has led to increased attention to issues such as animal welfare in agriculture and working conditions in the textile sector, and this 10% will also help to ensure that globalisation develops in an acceptable direction. thirdly, give consumers a voice, support consumer organisations, particularly in the candidate countries, and look for new ways of making consumers less anonymous. experiment also with public councils where consumers participate in the development of new production techniques and methods. my final point concerns political responsibility. a strong consumer policy should of course help to ensure that consumers are the focal point of european policy, from chemicals policy to electronic commerce. in europe, a great deal is done in the name of the consumer. liberalisation of public services would provide consumers with cheaper and better services. it's wonderful, of course, but what has it done? travelers all over europe are complaining about the declining quality of public transport. the telephone market has become a price-setting machine. and ultimately, few consumers have to choose between electricity suppliers. ten years of the single market, what has that done for consumers? or take the euro, another example. the euro would make everything cheaper. we now know that the euro has caused a considerable rise in prices. of course it can backfire. every consumer understands that. but if liberalisation, the euro and the single market do not have the desired effect, where can the consumer turn? can consumers turn to european politicians, national governments and businesses? or nowhere? consumers must have rights, but they must also be able to make political statements. in short, we must stop making vague promises to and about consumers. the objectives for consumers must be concrete and clear, and it must be clear who bears the political responsibility. thank you, sir.
- mr president, there are of course three important reports. it is not legislation, but i look forward to the legislation that will follow. i do so with great confidence, because on this point too we have full confidence in this commissioner. i am curious to see if he can give us a time frame for the proposals for legislation. the challenge is, of course, to ensure that consumer policy is properly aligned with the completion of the internal market. consumer policy should not be an excuse for the creation of barriers to trade. i also think that the figures the commissioner has just given on the benefits we all derive from harmonisation speak volumes in that respect. the consumer benefits from free trade by being able to buy cheaper and better products and we must of course achieve a high level of consumer protection. trust is the engine of economic growth. the consumer must have confidence in products, otherwise he will not buy them. industry must have confidence in the single market and consumers must have confidence in their suppliers. the knife cuts both ways. we must strive to ensure that consumers no longer have to choose whether they buy their products in the netherlands or in greece. it's not easy. consumers often do not know what their rights are. consumer organisations can help. consumer magazines are well read and contain useful tips. people have a lot of confidence in such organizations. i therefore believe - - mr president, when i was studying the three reports on consumer protection, i wondered whether this was not more about promoting consumerism. the single market is already a corollary of the 'you shall consume' command. it seems that there is now a need to add the commandment 'you shall consume throughout europe'. mr president, you will understand that i am rather critical of this. we cannot deny that language, distance and cultural differences are the main barriers to consumers. this is completely ignored by blaming the lack of familiarity with the regulations in other eu countries. in addition, we assume that the consumer is aware of the regulations in his own member state. if we want to invest in consumer confidence, we must first invest in the reliability of products and services. i believe that a well-informed consumer can make his own choices. this requires a balance between consumer protection and consumer responsibility. i do not think that a uniform legal framework is necessary. let us start with minimum standards in cases where there are real problems. it is forced to legislate on the basis of article 153 because this legal basis has only been applied in practice once. i am not afraid that we are discriminating against articles of the treaty by using them less than other articles.

in writing. - (nl) i agree with the majority who reject the proposal and my criticisms go a little further than his. each central bank makes important decisions on interest rates and exchange rates, thus influencing incomes, the employment sector, investment and the level of public facilities. it is precisely because of the importance of these decisions that the banks which issue banknotes have in the past been placed in the hands of the state. this has enabled important decisions to be taken away from the banks and put under the responsibility of the government and parliament. the european central bank risks becoming increasingly detached from the member states. there are significant risks that the central bank of issue will eventually behave as an institution totally independent of society and insulated from any control. a rotation system for the board of governors means that individual member state members are no longer involved in the decision-making process, while their country bears the negative consequences of these decisions. the enlargement of the eu and emu should not result in individual member states no longer having any commitments in this institution which is important for all the inhabitants of all the countries concerned. public control of the ecb must be intensified and not restricted.

mr president, the accession of new member states without precedent threatens to bring about an unprecedented conflict between the council and parliament. a balance of powers between the institutions is essential for the stability of cooperation within the eu. what the copenhagen summit decided in annex xv on the financial perspectives for the acceding countries affects the budgetary rights of this parliament as laid down in article 272 of the treaty. the council and parliament together form the budgetary authority and must respect each other in this. we also have the 1999 interinstitutional agreement for that. the unilateral adoption of the financial perspective is incompatible with this, even if it is understandable in the light of the situation at the end of the accession negotiations. we have no hidden agenda on this issue. we do not want to jeopardize the interinstitutional agreement, much less the signing of the accession treaties. but it seems that the council is doing so by undermining budgetary law, a vital prerogative of parliament. the presidency has informed us that it has not succeeded in removing annex xv because it concerns future primary legislation. article 272 of the treaty, budgetary law, is the primary law in force. as the two arms of the budgetary authority must meet each year, it is now, ideally tomorrow, but at least within two weeks, that we must reach out to each other. if we as the eu-15 fail to do so, we risk the eu-25.

and drug addiction reported that virtually all eu member states had developed alternative strategies. so they are not simply banning, but are trying to counter the harm of drug abuse by clever methods. i think that's the crux of it, too. different drugs have different user groups. a heroin addict often seeks oblivion, for example, cannot cope with life. but a guy who smokes a stick is usually not desperado. you and i are having wine with dinner tonight and many young people are using europe's second drug of pleasure, cannabis. ecstasy users are a very different group. that pill is part of a specific youth culture. their motto is: you know, you're gonna be all over the place on the weekend, but you're gonna be up early on monday. i therefore conclude that putting all drugs and drug users together will not solve the problem. i am also convinced that the strengthening of the prohibition will also increase the influence of organised crime. the netherlands is indeed an exporter of ecstasy, but it became so only after the dutch government fought it hard and it ended up in the hands of the big boys of the amphetamine mafia. the netherlands was too small a market for them and they started exporting it. i know that not all people in this house will share my analysis. how to deal with drug abuse and how to combat organised crime are subjects of political debate. but it must not be just about ideology and wishful thinking, but about reality, how to deal with reality and with the different realities. as rapporteur, i have chosen to write a recommendation which will help to advance this political debate. it was not my intention to take a position on the best way to combat drug abuse. instead, i have chosen - and this is supported by a majority of the committee on civil liberties and human rights - to advocate a thorough evaluation of the effectiveness of the un conventions on drugs. i would like to say to those who oppose my report - and i am speaking in particular for the ppe - that a call for an evaluation does not necessarily mean an adaptation of these un conventions. but we must be willing to look at those similarities. all those people who are convinced that a repressive approach really works so great have nothing to fear either, because they are likely to think that zero tolerance will be the outcome of such an evaluation and that this will now also be the recommendation that is made. i do not think it is the solution, but an evaluation will at least shed some light. i have been accused of extremism in discussions and i fully accept that label when it comes to my own ideas about dealing with drug abuse. we are in the midst of an important debate on the substance of the matter, and you can take my views as you wish. but i do not accept that label for this report. the essence of this report is a rational recommendation, an evaluation. an evaluation followed by a united nations conference in 2004 to discuss the conclusions. so it is a limited recommendation and i hope you can support it. a final point, mr president, concerns the classification of drugs. the evaluation will of course be long term, and in the short term it is important that we arrive at a reclassification of drugs. at the moment, cannabis and heroin are in the same category, and i think we can all agree that using heroin is more harmful than smoking a joint. i therefore propose that parliament should repeat what we already stated two months ago in the malliori report on the prevention and reduction of the risks associated with drug addiction, and thus call for a classification of drugs on the basis of scientific evidence of danger to human health.

that is to say, the official definition of our strategic concept, which in my view is far too limited. i am in favour of doing that first and then discussing, for example, what i consider to be a number of loose ends in mr morillon's report, namely territorial defence. we must now add them to the tasks of the european union? should we adopt article 5 of the weu treaty? in my opinion, that decision is premature. we are dealing with the strategic concept first, then we are looking at what we want to do with these european funds. it is too early for me to say that we should be able to take on a kosovo-like task in 2009. let's look at the strategic concept first and then take on those kinds of concrete tasks. secondly, another good point in the report concerns the misunderstanding which often prevails when we say - and i think the majority of this parliament is in favour of majority voting, including on security policy - then the european parliament cannot be excluded from the democratic control. we need effectiveness, but we would like it to be coupled with democratic control, and ultimately that will have to take place right here in this room.

mr president, vaccination cannot protect people in advance against new diseases. they can't be cured with medication afterwards either. there are only three ways to limit the impact. the first is to contain the risk of contamination. the second is to strengthen and accelerate scientific research to prevent and control such a disease. the third is to provide assistance to the sick to increase their chances of survival. in the fight against the sars outbreak, only that third possibility is now getting full attention. hospitals are being prepared for the availability of quarantine rooms and ventilation equipment. it is good that we are already considering the possibility that this contagion will strike europe in a large way, but it seems that we are limiting ourselves to that. the second option is less likely to succeed. in recent years, cutbacks have been made in scientific research into new diseases in several member states of the european union. today's experts are interested volunteers who are drawn to other medical and biological research. this must change if new diseases are to be effectively controlled and eradicated in the short term. the main shortcomings are in the first option, the containment of global spread. international air travel allows people from southeast asia to export sars over long distances at a rapid rate. the controls on incoming traffic at schiphol airport in the netherlands, the fifth largest airport in europe, are minimal. passengers from southeast asia can just walk through. it's actually a miracle that there aren't many more people the rapporteur. president, the nature and purpose of the instrument of macrofinancial assistance to third countries are good and useful. as regards policy effects, it should be noted that european community macrofinancial assistance contributes to economic reforms and structural changes in the recipient countries. such a useful instrument therefore deserves a sound legal basis. however, this is now missing. the current legal framework for the design, conditions for preparation, implementation, control, transparency and accountability of community macro-financial assistance is cumbersome and inefficient. the procedure at council level is very time-consuming. the current system is also ineffective, since the disbursement of funds can take up to two years. finally, there is no sound legal basis because the council insists on using article 308. what legal basis provides the necessary sound legal basis? article 181a would be the most logical option: economic, financial and technical cooperation with third countries. we are not in agreement with the council on this, which is not happy that macrofinancial assistance should be classified under 181a. the nice treaty will in due course be replaced by a new treaty, which is currently being discussed by the convention. the development of community macrofinancial assistance so far has been more budgetary than balance of payments assistance in terms of the way it is prepared, implemented, monitored and accountable. macro-financial assistance, as provided by the european institutions under the terms of the constitutional treaty, would fall under the provisions of article 28 on economic, financial and technical cooperation measures designed to respond to economic, financial or social crises. in addition, community macro-financial assistance should be subject to parliamentary scrutiny. the european parliament must therefore be given a vote. the draft article 28 provides for a normal legislative procedure with codecision, so i have no objections to this. this view of the legal basis is widely held in the european parliament. i hope that the council and the commission will share this view and thus give this good instrument the appropriate legal basis. we can then, as institutions, agree on transparency and effective criteria and their implementation. secondly, mr president, it is important to recognize that a solution must be found to the current ad hoc regime until the member states ratify the new constitutional treaty. the european parliament therefore considers it of great importance that the commission should submit a legislative proposal on the transitional period until the ratification of the new treaty. it should have a two-fold legal basis and meet two criteria: (a) macro-financial assistance shall be considered as assistance to third countries facing a crisis due to economic, financial or social circumstances; (b) decision-making based on codecision. the proposal will of course contain criteria for determining whether a country is eligible for aid. the council conclusions of 8 october 2002 on macrofinancial assistance, the so-called genval criteria, are useful and correct. they can serve as criteria within the future legal instrument if a number of amendments are respected. this is partly because of the exceptional nature of the case. the discontinuity clause must be maintained. the complementarity criterion has three caveats. first of all: an independent quantitative assessment by the commission. in addition, careful coordination with other community instruments in the framework of a political dialogue with the host country. thirdly, macro-financial assistance is complementary to the resources provided by the imf and other multilateral institutions. this does not, of course, preclude the eu from having its own position. conditionality is the interdependence between the economy of the receiving country and that of the eu. measurable macroeconomic criteria and reforms in the recipient country are also crucial. the european parliament's seriousness in improving the instrument is shown by the fact that the european parliament will consider suspending the adoption of budgetary appropriations in relation to macro-financial assistance until an adequate legislative proposal has been submitted. we all hope, of course, that the european parliament will not the rapporteur. president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking the shadow rapporteurs, mr goodwill of the christian democrats, mr langen of the socialists and mrs thors of the liberals. we worked well together. sulphur in marine fuel, it sounds technical and boring, but it's very important both for acidification and for human health. by the year 2010, nearly as much sulphur will come from ships as from all other land sources combined. that's because we've done so much on the land, in the big chimneys of factories and power plants, but also in the cars. in a few years, we'll be down to 10 ppm. but for seagoing vessels, it's 27,000 ppm, which is almost 3,000 times as much for seagoing vessels as for automobiles. acidification is still a major problem. in my own country, the netherlands, for example, only 10% of nature is protected against acidification. 90% is not. heaths are still turning into grasslands. vulnerable nature is still being destroyed. i am therefore very pleased that we have reached a compromise with all the political groups which goes far beyond what the european commission wants. we propose to move to 0.5% in two stages. we must not then take the problem of acidification seriously. the other reason we want to go this far is public health. the ships are emitting black carcinogenic particles, and those particles are being carried by the wind for 50, 100, even hundreds of kilometers. this is an aspect which the european commission has neglected. that is why we think the proposal to go back to 1.5% is too weak. i would ask commissioner wallström to really look into this matter and to go along with what the european parliament is proposing. we'll clean those ships in one go and not do half the work. how do we get to that 0.5% threshold? that's ambitious indeed. reducing the sulphur content from 3 to 1.5% can be done by the oil refineries without too much extreme cost. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's fishing fleet is not affected by the crisis. the commissioner has already said: the shipping industry is a very competitive business. it is therefore very gratifying that a company like p&o has already fitted one of its large ferries with a washing machine, or in english a scrubber. and it only cost 1.5 million euros, which is a bargain. this will remove 95% of sulphur and 80% of carcinogenic particles, and also reduce nox emissions by 10 to 20%. that thing is called an eco-silencer, which is because it also reduces noise a lot. i think this technique -- washing -- works well. as early as 1988, a ship in norway had the first such system installed. but we have incorporated in parliament's amendments that a test must be carried out first to make sure that the system really works well. only after that trial is successful do we want to open this path, including an emissions trading system so that it becomes possible for companies to equip one after another of their ships with such a new system instead of all at once. if they all had to be equipped at the same time, or if we all went to 0.5% in terms of bunker oil at the same time, that would be much more expensive. it's cheaper to have a carbon trading system like this. in short, ecology and economics go hand in hand. so, commissioner wallström, dive in again and go with parliament to 0.5%. there's one final reason why it's important to do something about these particles. many climate scientists say that these particles also have a negative impact on the climate. all seagoing vessels together account for 20% of those particles. this aspect must also be taken into account. that's a third reason to go beyond 1.5 and go to 0.5 percent.

in writing. -{nl) for a century, electricity generation and distribution remained essentially non-commercial business. it is not a product that you decide to buy or not to buy. every household needs electricity and no one can run the risk of not having it. the distribution is carried out by pipes under the public road. public services such as hospitals, schools and trams also consume a lot of electricity. this whole organization cannot be entrusted to a company which is motivated only by the lure of profit. it is best to entrust it to local or regional public monopolies, provided they are subject to democratic control by an elected parliamentary body that looks after the interests of the environment and consumers. we have a great deal of experience in the netherlands in the transfer of electricity supply to the private sector. green investments in small-scale electricity generation are neglected or crowded out in favour of importing nuclear power. today, the only thing that counts is electricity that can be produced or bought at a lower cost. paying for green electricity that consumers can buy from a different producer than their usual regional supplier most often leads to chaos. i support the rapporteur, mr turmes, in his attempt to counter the misinformation about the green electricity or the diversion of money for the dismantling of nuclear energy, but this is not enough.

the rapporteur. mr president, the following applies to turkey as a candidate country: the door is open, but the road is difficult. that is the message of my report. for the other candidate countries, this was a matter of course. they and their citizens also had a hard time getting to the finish line and until the last committee meetings they were the subject of clear-cut remarks urging completion of the work. turkey is no exception. there is therefore no reason to give this country special treatment because of its size or its strategic location. turkey has very different problems than the other candidates. these problems are mainly related to the political criteria of copenhagen. perhaps more than ever before, this report focuses on the background or deeper causes of the political failings, which often take the form of violations of the rights to classical liberties and of fundamental human rights. it is also because the turkish state is based on a philosophy developed in the 1920s, a period when europe did not have many pleasant examples to draw on. the criticisms of turkey concern the structures of the state, the dominant political position of the army, the military-dominated national security council, nationalism leading to the suppression of ethnic, religious and cultural minorities, and the priority of collective security and collective interests over individual human rights, which is a constant source of complaint. the military also has a very strong influence in education, broadcasting and business and it is very important that this is also partially recognised in turkey's latest reform packages. the question that always arises in any contact with turkey is: who are we talking to? are we talking to the government and the majority in parliament or are we actually talking to the representatives of what is called the deep state, the top generals and the high established bureaucracy? in addition to these problems, we also mention those on the borders, both those with cyprus and those with armenia and possibly with iraq. the lack of a functioning civil society is also striking. the trade union movement has little room. religious communities, including the muslim community, are under strict state control or are in difficulty. other candidates also had to make up for this shortfall. the aim of the candidate country is to develop into a member state like any other. for example, it should not matter in legal terms whether you live in diyarbakir or rotterdam. if that is the case, then membership cannot be sold to our citizens. a directly elected representative of the people may see that sooner and more consciously than a council of ministers. we therefore invite the council to be as clear in its policy towards turkey as this parliament and not to be tied to symbols and symbolic data. clearness has been the express aim of this report. it is not fair to conceal a series of objections out of a need for appreciation and then conjure them up again later. turkey must now know what is happening. that means radical changes, as other candidates have experienced. we therefore warmly welcome the intention to draw up a new constitution, expressing the wish that the political values which are also held in other member states should be taken as a starting point. the army must also be removed from its current dominant position and reduced to a form and function common to other member states. that has implications for the national security council and the state security courts. amendments to laws aimed at transforming a military nation, as i am told, into a civilian nation, must prove in practice that their objectives are being achieved. this is about mentality and culture. the union must therefore focus its support on the actual fulfilment of the political criteria, i.e. retraining and exchange programmes for civil servants, especially police officers, lawyers involved in the courts, etc. the torture, for example, must now be brought to an end and the return of displaced persons and refugees to their villages must not be impeded by the so-called village guards. religious freedom cannot be a dead letter. many frustrating government policies can in fact be abolished in a short time, and it is always surprising that they are not. cultural rights must be recognized not in a small way but with conviction and generosity. it seemed for a moment that the government could indeed establish its authority and we had also hoped that it could, for example, fulfil its intention to solve the cyprus problem on the basis of the un plan. unfortunately, that didn't work out. a successful attempt to do so again will have to prove that the army is indeed fulfilling its normal role. mr president, i am pleased to see the broad support for the report in this parliament. i have also looked at the amendments with a generous eye and where it could provide a plus. we agreed with mr swoboda that we could accept an amendment from the radical and green side, which deals with turkey's willingness to fulfil its responsibilities in the reforms, as an addition, not as a replacement. if it is not to be added, we shall vote against it. but if it is presented as an addition, we can also say 'yes' to that. i hope, moreover, that the debate on religion, culture and politics will not be stifled by deletions in paragraph 3. because that is a paragraph that could end this discussion in a very good way.

in writing. - (nl) since industrialisation, food prices have been artificially kept low, so that it has also been possible to keep wages in industry at a low level. since then, farmers have been forced to produce more and more for ever-diminishing wages. the eu subsidy system was a means of increasing economies of scale and increasing yield per hectare. part of the lack of income of the farmers was compensated by the taxpayer's money. the survival of small farms and villages in southern europe has become largely dependent on subsidy policy. this is why they consider the current common agricultural policy to be the best the eu has to offer, even if they want a more equitable distribution key. they see any change as a violent attack on neoliberalism. they fear that a new system will only subsidize land acquisition and speculation and that it will no longer be possible to prevent rural depopulation. in northern europe, on the other hand, the majority of smallholders have already disappeared and public opinion views agricultural funds as a form of bureaucracy, financial waste and environmental degradation that must be stopped as soon as possible. i was and i agree with the need to move from a system that supports production to one that guarantees income and protects the landscape. however, the current proposal seems to be aimed primarily at winning the good graces of the americans in the wto, to the benefit of exports of other eu products.
in writing. -(nl) when commissioner fischler announced the new agricultural policy on 10 july 2002, my first comment was: "a justified break with the past, but certainly not a solution for the victims". the reform was presented as a reward for those working on food quality and safety, to improve environmental and consumer protection. the maintenance and improvement of the rural situation had to be somewhat freed from the aspiration to an ever more intensive production. my party, the socialist party of the netherlands, has always called for this change. the agricultural organisations and farmers' representatives in the ep expressed their dissatisfaction. and rightly so, because the possibility of large groups of farmers leaving is again high. not only the small farmers in france, spain and greece, but also the large farmers in the netherlands, who are currently heavily dependent on bank loans. their income is not very high in relation to their work and the money invested, and for some of them the decrease in income may be considerable. farmers can only achieve livelihood security if we have the courage to break with the logic of free trade and reward them for landscape management, environmental protection and food security. otherwise, they will be forced to produce at lower prices than the us and other eu competitors, due to intensification, land depletion and export subsidies.

mr president, the frontiers in the third world are largely a product of european colonial governance. people who wanted to stay together have been divided because their territory was divided among colonial occupiers. on the other hand, nations that want to have an independent state are assigned to large powerful neighbors who make their home territory a wingwest. especially when metals or oil are found in the soil of such an area, it is difficult to change the political classification in a peaceful way. indonesia is a product of more than three centuries of dutch colonialism. five large islands and countless smaller ones have been brought together under one administration to supply cheap raw materials and merchandise to what the 19th-century writer multatuli called a north sea predatory state. the two areas where the indonesian military is now trying to crush separatist movements, aceh in north sumatra and west papua, are the latest to be added to the dutch colonial empire. it was not until about 1900 that they were occupied by the dutch colonial army, and in aceh a long and bloody war preceded this. the island of new guinea, which was originally divided between the netherlands, germany, and great britain and inhabited by the then still living ancient papuans, was of little interest to the dutch until indonesia broke away from the netherlands in the war of independence. back then, this was the last colonial outpost in asia. under pressure from america, which sought good relations with indonesia, the netherlands had to give up this territory 40 years ago. the promised referendum for the people on whether or not to join indonesia never happened. in 1945, the netherlands tried to divide indonesia into an independent, densely populated java and a number of satellite states connected to the netherlands. many indonesians, and certainly their rulers and military, still consider it a great success that they made that partition impossible. the powerful role of the indonesian military, which has for many years guarded the mines and oppressed ethnic minorities, is explained by this, as is the long-term occupation of former portuguese timor and an earlier attempt to incorporate former british malaysia. the problem in indonesia is caused by europe and america. it is therefore right that the european parliament should also intervene in these abuses. unlike in the past, this cannot be done through military intervention from outside, but must be done through diplomatic and, if necessary, economic pressure. the european union is not only a political force, but also a political force.
the political fragility of the indonesian federation is evident. the proverbial emerald belt is threatening to crumble in the far east, papua, and in the west, atjeh. the countermeasures, especially military ones, from jakarta have had a negative effect to date. in both papua and aceh they are undermining the autonomy promises of the central authority. that is a dangerous radicalization. the dutch are well aware that the escalation of the long-running conflict between jakarta and gam rebels, particularly in aceh, which has always been very much attached to its independence, could lead to a new hotbed of international islamist terrorism. this frightening prospect should move jakarta to act with tact. the commission and the council must be involved.

commission. mr president, first of all, a special thank you goes to the rapporteur, mr lisi, for his valuable work on this proposal. as you are aware, the commission proposal under discussion seeks to broaden the scope of the seveso ii directive in the light of the baia mare and enschede accidents. furthermore, it seeks to incorporate the recommendations of two studies, one dealing with carcinogens and the other with substances which are dangerous to the aquatic environment. whilst the commission proposal did not originally contain measures related to the toulouse accident, a number of amendments proposed by parliament have been incorporated into the commission’s amended proposal and subsequently into the council’s common position. i would like to stress again that it was not the intention of the commission to effect a major overhaul of the seveso ii directive. i shall now comment on some of the proposed amendments. amendments nos 9 to 11 on risk mapping and potassium nitrate were already accepted by the commission during the first reading and consequently they figure in the commission’s amended proposal. these were the only three amendments that were fully rejected by the council when adopting its common position. the commission continues to support these amendments and can furthermore accept amendment no 8 related to training for emergencies. i am pleased to tell you that a proposal for a directive on the management of mining waste was adopted by the commission on 2 june 2003. the measures in the proposal complement those outlined in the seveso ii directive and include the establishment of a major accident prevention policy and a safety management system. these measures will apply to those waste management facilities that present an accident risk but will not be covered by the revised seveso ii directive. in our opinion, the seveso ii directive should only apply to the most dangerous mining activities where chemical processes are involved and chemical substances are stored on site. the seveso ii directive should not be transformed into either mining legislation or waste legislation. therefore the commission cannot agree to deleting the words ‘chemical and thermal’ as proposed in amendments nos 1 and 2. we also reject amendment no 12 which proposes making a reference to council directive 91/689/eec on hazardous waste, and amendment no 13, which seems to suggest that there are gaps in the coverage of mining sites through the two proposals. in our opinion this is not the case. amendments nos 3 and 4 would lead to requiring operators of seveso lower-tier sites to include information on training measures in the notification and to inform the competent authority in the event of a modification of an installation, establishment or storage area. in our view this would introduce bureacratic burdens without improving safety. a notification should only provide certain minimum information. the issue of training is already appropriately addressed in the directive; moreover, in the event of modifications, the reviews of the major accident prevention policy and the safety management system are important, not the notification. i acknowledge parliament’s strong wish to reinforce article 12 of the seveso ii directive. however, the commission and the council have already accepted related amendments presented in the first reading. amendment no 6 does not constitute an added value; on the contrary, there is no need for separate guidelines setting out a methodology on minimum safety distances, as it should be possible to derive these distances from the technical database that will be created as a tool to help assess the compatibility between seveso sites and sensitive sites. furthermore, the commission continues to be of the opinion that a development of incentive schemes and/or funding for the relocation of establishments is a task for member states – this is subsidiarity. the commission cannot, therefore, accept amendment no 7. to conclude, let me confirm the commission’s position on all amendments. the commission accepts amendments nos 8 to 11. amendments nos 1 to 7 and amendments nos 12 and 13 are not acceptable. i would like to emphasise that it is in our common interest to have this proposal adopted and implemented as quickly as possible.

in writing. - (nl) public procurement has long been regarded as a miracle cure. on the one hand, they are an alternative to nepotism and the awarding of contracts by governments to entrepreneurs who are friends of politicians or other high-ranking officials. they are also intended to stop the production and supply of services by government-owned enterprises and thereby allow private enterprises to access new markets. i already stated at the first reading on 17 january 2002 that i could accept the first purpose of these tenders but not the second. this second purpose makes governments increasingly dependent on business. the damage can only be limited by various bureaucratic rules, but these rules will remain unknown to many and will therefore be cheerfully broken. the dutch employers' association vno-ncw even asked not to extend the scope of the procurement directives by "a whole series of social and ecological criteria". it considers that the award procedure is 'a purely economic process which should not be disturbed in order to achieve other objectives'. the rapporteur has already himself dealt with a number of points in the field of social and environmental protection. i reject that approach. that said, i agree with the rapporteur that the theoretical market does not operate across borders and therefore does not have free competition. it is therefore better not to set rules on the assumption that this is indeed the case.
in writing. - (nl) the objections raised against mr zappalà's report on public contracts for works, supplies and services apply even more to this directive, which is being dealt with at the same time. these are large-scale, sustainable markets and tasks which for a century or more have been considered as the main tasks of government itself. these are goods and services which are indispensable to society as a whole, to households and businesses, and which in the past have been deliberately taken out of the hands of private enterprises. these companies had failed to provide continuity, quality services, acceptable prices and proper treatment of the consumer. a government monopoly under democratic control was considered the only acceptable solution to guarantee the desired product and consumer protection. this choice was then hardly disputed, even by the defenders of capitalism. as regards supplies and services in this field, private enterprises preferred to rely on a reliably functioning state monopoly rather than the uncertainty and lack of continuity that characterise the free market. meanwhile, governments that want to reduce their taxes and need money have sold these companies to international consortia that are willing to profit from them. if we choose such a solution, rules are absolutely necessary. but there is little to consider about corporate secrets and other interests.

in writing. - (nl) my group's view is that the outcome of the convention is not a good starting point for the forthcoming igc. one of the main reasons for this is that the preamble distorts the history of europe: christianity is deliberately not mentioned, even though it has profoundly influenced and shaped the culture and politics of all european countries for centuries. for the 'european house' to be strong, it must be built on sound foundations. in its conclusions on the middle east, the council reminded both parties of their obligations. it is a pity that the eu has not always firmly supported this view. the views expressed on terrorist organisations such as hamas - their relations with the countries of the region and the financing of their abominable actions - are not to be minced. the conclusions on iran and lebanon, in the light of the agreements the eu wishes to conclude with these countries, are unfortunately not as firm. this text reveals the inconsistency of the eu's attitude and makes it an unpredictable party for israel and other countries in the region. the opening of internal borders requires member states to cooperate on asylum and immigration. there was much work to be done in this regard in thessalonica, but the results were disappointing. the uk plan to set up enrolment and reception centres in the region was not approved by the majority of the council. the pilot project that can be launched is a small consolation prize. it is high time that the council achieved results so that the eu can live up to its moral obligations towards political refugees.
in writing. - (nl) economies of scale have disadvantages but are sometimes necessary. this principle certainly holds true for long-distance travel. this type of traffic crosses national borders, so that its safety and regulation are the responsibility of more than one state. in the past, this would have led to plans for the formation of a single european railway company and then a single european airline with a single air traffic safety system. it is clear that these monopolies should have been subject to democratic control to avoid abuse of power, waste and favoritism. meanwhile, neoliberal ideology has struck. not only the services but also the maintenance of the supporting infrastructure and the control of security can be entrusted to competing companies. the tasks financed with public money have to be allocated on the basis of the principle of competition and the jobs become uncertain, which is a major concern for those responsible for this work. it is good that national borders and military zones are losing their significance in the organisation of aviation security, but this does not mean that the present presentation of aviation security is the best. last night we were pleasantly surprised to learn that commissioner de palacio would make it clear during this debate that this proposal was not in any way aimed at privatising or liberalising the sector. i fear, however, that in the long run it may be unintentionally used for this purpose.
in writing. - (nl) the passage of goods by road through the alps is a recurring stumbling block in this area as elsewhere. i took part in the debate or gave explanations of vote on 15 december 1999, 14 december 2000, 4 september 2001 and 11 and 12 february 2003. the germans and italians are calling for freedom of passage through austria and switzerland, but both countries want to protect their valleys from these heavy goods flows and want to move this type of transport quickly to railways. i support the efforts of both countries in this regard. switzerland complies with eu regulations and also participates in the european economic area. however, she does not pay or vote. it cannot therefore be made into a minority by others. austria, unlike switzerland, has the misfortune of being a member of the eu for eight years. others therefore believe that it is possible to impose their will on him. they even want to end the distribution of ecopoints altogether. let us instead equip the brenner base tunnel for electric rail transport under austria, so that germany and italy will become neighbours in practice and will no longer disturb the small countries between them. as in previous occasions, my vote will be in favour of the austrian members of parliament as they defend their quality of life against a total lack of vision.

in writing. - (nl) the debate on the annual report of the european central bank and the visit of the president of the ecb are the only times in the year when the impression is not that the issuing bank of 12 of the 15 member states is being privatised. whereas in the past these banks were nationalised in order to further politicize their policies, politics is now kept at a distance. interest rates, exchange rates, the impact on vulnerable regions, relations with the united states of america and the position of the third world are thus largely determined outside the scope of parliamentary democracy. this also applies to the influence of the ecb and the stability pact on pensions, social security and the level of public benefits. the rapporteur, mr blokland, rightly points out that the success or failure of the euro can be measured not only by the speed with which euro banknotes and coins are introduced at the beginning of 2002, but also by the increase in the price of services. i am happy to support him in his desire to make public the inflation forecasts, the influence exercised by the governments of the member states and, above all, the minutes of all meetings of the governing council, including minority views and the distribution of votes, and to increase the influence of parliament on the composition of the governing council. only then will we avoid the ecb becoming an instrument at odds with the majority of the eu's citizens.
in writing. - (nl) the strengthening of the measures proposed by the rapporteur runs counter to the experience gained in the past. for both germany and france, the large member states that initiated the euro, and the economically weaker southern member states, it seems practically impossible to meet the strict conditions of the stability pact. combining tax cuts with reducing public debts while avoiding new budget deficits has devastating consequences for social security, public services and the ability of governments in general to solve problems. there will soon be no money left in any area where democracy requires active commitment from the authorities. the weak regions are increasingly dependent on the eu's structural funds, cohesion funds and common agricultural policy, for which, proportionately, the amounts committed are steadily decreasing over time. the rapporteur is right to want to avoid price increases when the euro is introduced in new member states of the euro area. in fact, they already exist because payment for luxury goods and services is already often made in euros rather than in the national currencies that are still in use. in practice, the elimination of the lower value coins, which is also advocated, will lead to greater price increases, as rounding upwards will become the norm. that is why i reject this measure.

international shipping has been in rough waters for several decades. globalisation has considerably increased the pressure on various parts of the sector. both the construction and operation of the ships had to be less expensive. the community's flag states have revised their conditions, particularly under the influence of 'cheap' registers. in addition, the western fleet is faced with a declining number of 'native' qualified seafarers. the commission has also decided to extend the scope of the programme to include the following areas: each country arranged this separately, resulting in a lot of double work and taxation of the bureaucracy. that is why we are in principle in favour of this proposal. the central coordination of the recognition of training and the associated certificates is a step forward. in doing so, we must not lose sight of a number of things. firstly, there is the need to make adequate use of the european maritime know-how and manpower available. the amendment of the current system must not lead to the exclusion of non-community personnel from the labour market of the member states, with all the consequences for the recruitment and training of new seafarers in the european union. this should be duly taken into account in the recognition of certificates of competency issued by a third country. secondly, the authorization must not be the end of the operation. training is a human endeavour and subject to change. all the criteria for recognition must be checked at regular intervals, both before and during the period of recognition. otherwise, the license will have to be revoked, without pardon. i believe that the maritime agency has an important role to play in this process. in short, this proposal can do away with a lot of unnecessary work, but caution is warranted in its enforcement and implementation. we can therefore support this proposal provided that the above points are adequately covered.

first stage is fever and weakness. the disease is then difficult to detect, but relatively easy to treat. if left untreated, the parasite can travel from the bloodstream to the brain. it can take several weeks to years for the disease to progress from stage 1 to stage 2. stage two is when seizures and convulsions begin. stage two sleeping sickness is easy to recognize, but treatment is much more difficult. if the disease is not treated, the patient falls into a coma, and death is inevitable. this treatment is usually lacking in developing countries. many people die needlessly because in writing. - (nl) recognising linguistic diversity within the eu is not a matter of folklore. currently, 40 million eu citizens speak a language other than their official national language; it's going to be 46 million next year. for the children and grandchildren of migrants, the language of the environment will be the first language spoken. this does not apply to stateless peoples or to those living in "pockets" separated by a border from speakers of the same language. europe has been the scene of a long battle to enable education, administration and work in the national language of its citizens. citizens deprived of this opportunity become second-class citizens. first-class citizens are those who speak the dominant language in private or who are fully adapted to it. within the eu, there is a growing contrast between peoples who have their own member states and those who are treated as minorities in states where the majority language is different. the language of the latter group is still not recognised within the eu, unless it is the same as that of a neighbouring state. for example, the ten million catalan speakers will continue to wonder why their language is less important than that of much smaller language groups such as the danes, finns, the baltic peoples and the slovenes. if we do not find a solution in time, we will face major conflicts.
