president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, i share the view of mr rocard and mr cappato and other members who believe that software as such should not be patentable. article 52 of the european patent convention excludes software as such and says that ideas and principles are not suitable for patenting. it must be about technical inventiveness and that is precisely the crux of the problem we all face. it is also the point of the directive. meanwhile, the patent office has concluded that all programs running on a computer are by definition technical. we now have an existing practice where the patent office has already granted over thirty thousand patents, many of which are actually not legally valid. mr rocard rightly pointed out that there is a difference between an invention based on natural forces and a product of the human mind. i think that this is why we should support some of the amendments which have already been tabled in the committee on industry and also the amendments tabled in the committee on culture in the past. these give such a tightening of the definition that in my view software as such is excluded. if these amendments are not adopted, i shall vote against the directive. colleagues, there is a great deal of unrest in the small and medium-sized business and open source movement. human knowledge, and the dissemination of it, is a great freedom that we must preserve in europe. it is only because of human dignity that this is required, but not only for that reason. we will be even more competitive than the americans and the directive will have to exclude american states absolutely. i hope that many will vote along these lines, so that we can have a directive that is workable.
mr president, commissioner, our starting point is also that we do not think that patents are the right way of protecting inventions implemented in computers. until now, copyright has provided reasonable protection for this. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area, and it is not surprising that the commission has taken a number of initiatives in this area. unfortunately, this debate has been rendered obsolete by the practice of the european patent office. this agency has been issuing so-called software patents for years and these have been enforced to the highest national level. the proposal now before us is really a kind of emergency measure to keep the granting of patents in europe within certain limits. i sympathize with that. but the question is, does it make sense? the european patent office has already granted 30,000 patents on the basis of regulations which go beyond the current proposal for a directive. so in that respect, the directive seems like mustard after the meal. the positive thing is that the directive will lead to harmonisation and clarity in the member states. but the danger of small innovative firms being destroyed by the monopolies of the big ones remains. that's inherent in the patent system. we are well aware of that. we are therefore disturbed by the fact that the commission and the rapporteur are laconically passing this over. it shows little affinity with european small and mediumsized enterprises, the backbone of our economy.
in writing. -{nl) today we have to choose a new president of the european central bank, but in reality we have no real choice. from the outset, the aim was for the bank to be located in germany and run by a frenchman. as the dutchman wim duisenberg had done the preparatory work for the ecb, he was eventually elected president for a short period. when he was appointed, it was known that a compromise had been reached, namely that the eight-year term of office would be shared between mr duisenberg and mr trichet. from the outset, mr trichet was therefore guaranteed to obtain the post, even if only for half the period. it almost went wrong when it appeared that mr trichet might go to prison. it has now been suggested that his mandate be extended for a further eight years. the argument currently put forward in favour of his appointment is that, unlike his country's government, he will strictly observe the 3% deficit threshold provided for in the stability pact. this seems to be a path that leads straight to disaster. large member states cannot do it, and poor member states will certainly not be able to do it. in the netherlands, a country that respects this ceiling, everything of value is reduced to nothing. in this context, i see no reason to approve mr trichet's candidacy.
in writing. - (nl) the world is paying the price for wanting to keep shipping artificially cheap. ships from rich countries fly the flag of poor countries with minimal taxation and minimal protection for crews who are paid at the rates of developing countries. ships are inspected on a commercial basis by different agencies which compete with each other and fear losing their customers if they are too strict. maritime countries try to limit the problem of cargo losses and maritime disasters by keeping transport as far as possible from their coasts in which they have no direct interests at stake. in the case of the prestige oil tanker which sank off the coast of galicia, the disaster was aggravated by the spanish authorities' attempt to push the ship away from the coast instead of safely taking it into port. today, six months after the disaster, oil continues to leak from the sunken wreckage. the spanish government is persisting in its mismanagement and the rapporteur has obviously decided to ignore it. i support his proposals to promote the safety of port facilities, to make pilot guidance compulsory, to encourage research, to avoid criminalising seafarers, to make the polluter pay compensation and to provide funds for cleaning up oil-covered animals. however, these measures will remain inadequate as long as airlines seek maximum profits and countries try to keep costs as low as possible.

in writing. - (nl) in america, the big computer companies have been trying for years to protect their software inventions from free use by individual users and small businesses. they impose technical restrictions, force buyers to enter into restrictive contracts, seek high damages and require legal protection from the authorities. as a result, it is the young and resourceful users who face increasing restrictions and the risk of being imprisoned. in europe too, companies of this type are trying to protect their monopoly better against the public. in derogation from article 52 of the european patent convention, which subjects software not to patent law but to copyright, the european patent office in munich is trying to broaden its powers by moving in the same direction as the us system. this has resulted in the granting of 30,000 patents to date. the european commission and a section of this parliament want to justify this extension of powers by arguing that nothing is actually changing in relation to the current situation. this attitude - with good reason - is much opposed by those who find it impeded in their inventions, teaching, work or leisure. i support this opposition to the commercial interests of the big monopolies and i had the pleasure of collaborating before this vote in the development of counter-arguments.
in writing. - (nl) the introduction of pension schemes was once considered a step forward in the direction of a civilized society. together, we were building our future, to ensure security in an age when people are no longer productive. today, the view is widespread that pension obligations are a burden on society and that the elderly exploit the generations. on the one hand, this is a consequence of the altered age pyramid, which is becoming much narrower than before, as there are fewer young people at the bottom and more older people at the top. but it is also linked to a tendency to think short-term, to an incentive to individual selfishness and to the emergence of individual-type pension plans. young people rarely realise that they will live long after their peak productivity. they also often fail to realize that people are getting tired because work becomes a form of high-level sport. the expectations of workers' productivity are so high that many of them are physically or psychologically worn out before they reach retirement age. employers often no longer want employees over 55. however, people in this age group are often useful as volunteers, consultants or childcare workers. in the circumstances, it would be more sensible to lower the retirement age rather than to raise it. refusing to give pensions to people who are no longer able to cope with the pressure of work creates insoluble problems.
in writing. - (nl) like many national constitutions, the draft constitution is charmingly rhetorical on several points, such as a high level of environmental protection, some vaguely social points and the rejection of the death penalty and discrimination. however, this text was not originally designed for this purpose. the real important points are the strengthening of the power of the council, which impedes parliamentary democracy, the integration of the whole eu into nato and the establishment of the capitalist character of the eu economy. there will soon be no place for a militarily neutral position outside nato, as adopted to date by sweden, finland, ireland, austria, cyprus and malta. it is not just about defending each other's territory against external enemies, but also about the ability to intervene outside nato and eu territory to defend our own interests. the constitution also protects freedom of enterprise and 'pure and free competition'. in our neoliberal europe, public utility companies in the public transport, postal, energy and telecommunications sectors are no longer considered to be entrusted with essential community tasks, but are handed over to operators who seek to make a profit. this constitution will be similar to that of cuba or the former soviet union, which also wanted to define the type of their economy in a lasting way and protect it from democratic decisions of change. if europe is to have a constitution, this is not the right text. a referendum must be held in each member state on this issue.

president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i too would like to congratulate mr van velzen on his hard work as rapporteur. he dragged out what was inside. every citizen in europe has the right to access information collected and stored by public authorities. after all, transparency on the part of the public authorities is good for democracy, and democracy is not paid for in europe. in addition, government information also has important economic potential. the directive should lead to a vibrant trade in government information in the european union, as in the united states. there is a huge potential gap which, if exploited commercially, could create many jobs, particularly in smes and small and medium-sized enterprises. i therefore see a central role for the government in this as a catalyst for a new market. the commission has put forward an ambitious proposal. but for some member states the latter is apparently less interesting. they have so watered down the proposal that it is questionable whether the internal market for government information will work in the longer term, let alone in the short term. member states were not prepared to make public information available free of charge, while there was constant talk of e-europe and the information society for all. that's a great line. if you say "a", you must say "b". for information which is publicly available, it is self-evident that the marginal costs of reproduction and distribution may be passed on. now, however, the costs may be increased by "a reasonable profit margin". that is undesirable, because it creates unlimited opportunities for the government to make profits. because who decides what's reasonable? the proposal further draws on government documents rather than government information. this does not guarantee that information displayed electronically also falls within the definition. the public authorities are tempted to restrict access to printed documents. easy access to public information, preferably via the internet, reduces the distance between the european public authorities and the citizens. governments should therefore be encouraged to make as many documents available to citizens as possible by electronic means. this is a crucial prerequisite for the emergence of e-europe, an information society for all.

i would like to begin by thanking the rapporteur for his work on the transport line. the execution directive is an important environmental directive. solvents are one of the main causes of ozone formation and this has serious consequences. first of all, for public health, respiratory and respiratory diseases are caused by the emission of volatile organic compounds. plant growth and crops are also affected. we are rightly setting limits on solvents, and those limits can be made even stricter for my group. the study carried out by the commission shows that environmental gains could be further increased by setting somewhat more ambitious limit values. that is why our group is calling for a reduction in the limit values, in line with the study carried out by the commission. we certainly do not agree with the rapporteur's and the previous speaker's view that less solvent means less quality. experience in a number of countries has shown that even with less solvent europe can maintain a good quality and beautiful colour. the paint industry has been through a strong innovation precisely because of the limits that have been set and the end point is far from being reached. i am firmly convinced that innovation is also the basis of employment. the pse group also has a point of principle. there's no mention of painter's disease in the execution line. like there's no people working with paint, like there's no painters holding the brush every day. painter's disease is a disorder of the nervous system. exposure to solvents can have serious consequences, such as memory and concentration loss and premature dementia. some countries have taken measures to protect painters from the disease by allowing solvents and encouraging the wise use of paint. these measures have produced good results. this is a possibility which should not be denied to any member state, either now or in the future. the directive on the enforcement of the directive is a harmonization directive and will undoubtedly be a good thing for industry, which wants clear and unambiguous rules in the internal market. however, harmonization must not be at the expense of social achievements. the consequence of this directive would be that member states who wish to do so would no longer be able to pursue their national policies, and that is absolutely unacceptable to my group. that is why we have tabled proposals to correct this mistake. let me be very clear here: if the single market means that trade unions are denied the right and the opportunity to advocate better working conditions, then my group will vote 'no'. i must say, commissioner, that i am rather surprised that we should be having a debate on this at all. the european union has been advocating sustainable development for many years. the starting point of sustainable development is to reconcile economic, environmental and social aspects. since johannesburg, the whole world has agreed on the need for sustainable development and the need to put it into practice. unfortunately, the best opportunity to combine economic, social and environmental objectives is now the first, and the social objective is not out of the question. i therefore urge the rapporteur to look again at the various amendments which strengthen the social aspect of the directive and to support them. i agree with several colleagues from different groups that this is a too one-sided internal market directive. the social veneer is really too thin to provide any real protection. working conditions should be much better.
mr president, the volatile organic compounds in solvents which cause ozone pollution are released particularly when cars are sprayed, but also when houses are painted on the outside of their wooden walls. the european commission is rightly proposing a revision of the existing directive to reduce this air pollution. the time-limits for meeting standards are very long. the economic arguments seem to have prevailed. the preparation of this revised directive has clearly revealed conflicts of interest. the trade union movement, particularly the european building and woodworking union, has experience of the painter's disease ops, which is caused by solvents that affect the central nervous system. in a small country like the netherlands, where the law has severely restricted the use of volatile organic substances since 1 january 2000, several thousand workers still suffer from this serious disease which they contracted in the past. the fact that there are no more victims is due to the low limit values, which for many products have set the standard at a maximum of 100 grams of solvent per litre of paint, and to the mandatory substitution of alternative products. there is a fear that a uniform system at eu level, which is less stringent than the dutch one, will contribute to the increase in the number of victims in the netherlands. what is wrong with protecting all eu countries as much as the member state with the most extensive measures, so that people working with paint can remain healthy everywhere? the commission has already taken a number of measures to protect the health of workers in the community. the industry wants harmonization and stability above all. international companies want to be exempted from the obligation to take individual measures for each member state. they feel that the existing rules are not already being monitored and respected and use that as an argument to reject stricter rules. the commission has also proposed that the standards be set for many years to come, without any further tightening. they believe that the environment would benefit from the use of more aggressive materials, which would reduce the need for repainting. they also claim that the european commission and its officials have always promised that this directive would only deal with emissions into the environment and not with the protection of the safety and health of people at work. i have already said that the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. firstly, to maintain national protection measures for workers as long as eu standards are less stringent and secondly to improve the eu standards currently proposed. in a number of amendments i propose that the standards of the decopaint study should at least be followed. this study was carried out at the request of the european commission but was unfortunately not included in the proposals. that mistake can be corrected now. moreover, we should not wait until 2010 to reduce the limit values, but do so as soon as possible.
the commission proposal is based on the scientific report on decopaint, which was commissioned by the european commission and which was prepared after a long and thorough investigation. i was therefore surprised, as were my colleagues, that the commission largely ignored the conclusions of this report. without giving reasons, newer higher limit values are proposed, which are not based on any research. what they're based on, there's no way to tell. i would like to hear commissioner wallström's explanation on this point. it is unacceptable that the commission should simply dismiss the conclusions of the decopaint report. i have therefore tabled amendments to correct this and will support other amendments which have the same objective. we are talking about substances that are not only dangerous for the environment but also for human health. exposure to these substances can lead to impairment of brain function and eventually to disability. in several member states, therefore, legal measures have been taken to curb this danger. it is important that this protection should continue, also in the new directive. the commission's present proposal does not provide for this possibility and therefore needs to be adapted in this respect. it can never be the aim of the commission to give workers less protection than is already being offered. it is very important that these measures should be allowed now and in the future. i therefore support the amendments in this respect. mr president, i would like to conclude by saying that this dossier is further proof of the close link between the environment and public health and that it is therefore wise that these subjects should be dealt with in the same committee in the next term.
commission. – mr president, firstly, i should have started by thanking mr lisi for his work as rapporteur on this important proposal. i do it now instead and hope he will forgive me for not doing so earlier. allow me to return to the question of the purpose and the scope of the proposal. a number of the amendments adopted by parliament's committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy are motivated by concern for the protection of the health of workers. some of these amendments – 10, 16 and 26 – aim to emphasise that the present proposal will not restrict or prejudice national or community measures established in order to protect the health of workers from exposure to solvents in paints and varnishes. the commission agrees with the principle underlying these amendments. measures for the protection of the health of workers fall outside the purpose and scope of this proposal, and the proposal therefore does not prejudice such measures in any way. the commission also agrees that it may be useful to clarify and emphasise this point directly in one of the paragraphs of the proposal. however, and for exactly the same reason, the commission cannot agree to include a number of amendments which directly or indirectly aim to enhance the protection of workers' and consumers' health from exposure to solvents in the paints and other products covered by the proposals – amendments nos 17, 20 and 23. the commission finds that these amendments, rather than reducing the risk for human health, might inadvertently serve to create confusion about the scope of the proposal. a number of the amendments voted by the committee – amendments nos 11, 13, 14, 32, 33 and 34 – contain useful technical clarifications with which the commission can agree to a greater or lesser degree. as an example let me just mention the proposal that the part of the vocs in the paint which reacts to form the coating film remaining on the painted surface should not be included when assessing compliance with the voc content limit value. that is amendment no 11. this makes sense from an environmental point of view, as it is the part of the vocs that evaporates into the atmosphere we want to reduce. however, there is a practical sticking point: for the time being we do not have any recognised standard or method for calculating the weight of those vocs which remain bound in the film. such a standard has to be developed in order to allow for this deduction. the commission also finds it reasonable to accept that member states, under strict conditions and in limited quantities, may grant derogations for special paints, as you mentioned, for the restoration and maintenance of vintage cars and historic buildings. that concerns amendments nos 6, 19 and 22. in total, the commission can, to a greater or lesser degree, accept 20 of the 83 amendments tabled for the vote in plenary tomorrow. of the remaining 63 amendments, which the commission cannot accept for different reasons, most are of a fairly technical nature. allow me to make only a few comments on these amendments and our reasons for rejecting them. four amendments – 5, 27, 81 and 83 – aim to oblige the commission to present tighter limit values and/or enlarge the scope of the present values at some later date. quite apart from the question of principle concerning the commission's right of initiative, we firmly believe that it would be unwise to guess at what we should do in four or five years in order to improve air quality. when we have the results of the clean air for europe programme in a couple of years, we will be in a much better position to assess if, where and what action might be needed in order to improve air quality in a scientifically and economically justified manner. amendment no 12 proposes enlarging the scope of the directive by including vocs with a boiling point – as several members have mentioned – up to 280°c rather than the 250°c proposed by the commission. this is not acceptable to the commission. firstly, because organic compounds with a boiling point above 250°c have a very low volatility: it takes several days for them to dry out and they have a very limited ozone formation potential. in other words, they are of little environmental concern. secondly, because 250°c is the boiling point chosen to define vocs in the eu eco-labelling scheme. it would be both inconsistent and bizarre to choose a stricter definition for this proposal. mr davies, b&q/kingfisher will be able to continue to use their labelling scheme. no less than 36 amendments – 36 to 53, 55 to 57, 59 to 63, 65, and 67 to 77 – aim to change the limit values proposed by the commission. the commission is aware that intense lobbying activities have been going on, both from industry and from environmental organisations, with a view to either softening or tightening the limit values proposed by the commission. however, so far the commission has not been presented with convincing evidence that the values of the proposal are not well balanced, economically justified and technically achievable within the deadlines proposed. therefore the commission, at this time, finds that it should stand by the limit values, procedures and deadlines proposed.

commission. – mr president, the oral question from mrs jackson and the draft resolution before parliament today on the same subject are all very timely. one year after our return from johannesburg we must keep up the momentum and maintain political leadership in the european union by delivering on our johannesburg commitments. i want to address the specific points in mrs jackson's oral question before taking the opportunity to add a few more general points on the johannesburg follow-up. let me start by addressing the last issue raised in mrs jackson's question: the commission's role in making sure that sustainable development becomes a major and regular aspect of forthcoming spring councils. i would like to make three points in response to this part of the question. first, by adding an external dimension to the göteborg strategy, the european council conclusions mean that the european union's sustainable development strategy is the main vehicle for the implementation of the johannesburg commitments. consistent with this approach, the commission intends to continue addressing the follow-up of the world summit in its annual synthesis reports in preparation for the spring european council meetings. second, the commission is also undertaking an overall review of the sustainable development strategy to be ready by the time the new commission takes up office. the review, covering the period up until 2009, will further integrate the world summit implementation into the revised strategy. third, the commission services are now preparing a stocktaking document on the summit follow-up that will be submitted by the end of 2003 and that may also include proposals for further action. we want parliament to be more closely involved in discussing the implementation of the world summit commitments. let me now turn to the first part of the oral question, reporting specifically on the water and energy initiatives. in our stocktaking paper on the world summit follow-up the commission plans to submit to parliament and to the council a detailed report on both initiatives. 'water for life' aims to bring sanitation and water to those who lack it most. currently 2.2 billion people die from water-related diseases each year, a figure that is unacceptable. the eu initiative is focused on africa, but will also cover other regions. a ministerial conference in addis ababa in december 2003 should help to develop ownership among all african stakeholders. the commission has tabled an ambitious proposal to allocate eur 1 billion from the european development fund to set up an eu water fund. this money is already reserved in the budget, but the council has so far been reluctant to free up the resources. the european union energy initiative for poverty eradication and sustainable development addresses access to affordable and sustainable energy services. nearly 30 developing countries from three continents have joined the initiative. to take it forward in africa the commission will sponsor a high-level energy event to be held in nairobi on 20 and 21 november 2003. as in the case of water, ownership and awareness in recipient countries are essential to make progress. still on the subject of energy, the eu also launched in johannesburg the renewable energy coalition. the commission has agreed to host the coalition secretariat. we intend to work intensively in the coming months to ensure the coalition is fully consolidated in time for the 2004 world renewable energy conference in germany. on the final part of the oral question dealing with strengthened governance for sustainable development, this is clearly an essential requirement for progress in the world summit implementation. in this regard, the european council has stressed the need to reinforce unep and to consider its institutional upgrading by creating a un environment agency. this is an important objective and our interaction with unep must be enhanced right away. in the short term we need to expand unep's role in the world summit implementation. the results of the global ministerial environment forum in february 2003 should help to achieve this objective. the results were very positive on chemicals, with a decision on the strategic approach to international chemicals management, setting up a process that should culminate in an intergovernmental conference in 2006. unep was also asked to take an active role in the pursuit of the ten-year framework of programmes on sustainable consumption and production, agreed in johannesburg. the global ministerial environment forum will meet again in korea in march 2004. water, sanitation and human settlements – the three items on the csd agenda for 2004 and 2005 – will be the main focus of discussions. nevertheless, some of the unfinished business on international environmental governance will also need to be addressed, including matters such as unep's funding, the reinforcement of its scientific basis and its role in enforcing international environmental agreements. let me turn to some of the broader issues associated with the world summit implementation and reflected in the draft resolution. one year ago i came to parliament and told you that the european union could be proud of the leadership role it played during the johannesburg summit. i also told you that our slogan for the summit would continue to guide us in the implementation phase: from words to deeds. my own assessment is that work is in progress to implement our commitments across the economic, social and environmental dimensions of sustainable development, both internally and externally, but events, and most recently the failure of the trade talks in cancún, show the scale of the challenge we still face. in march 2003 the european council identified a set of priorities for implementing the sustainable development strategy and the johannesburg outcomes. foremost amongst those priorities is policy coherence between external commitments and internal policies. the reform of the common agricultural policy and the fisheries policy is a step in the right direction. however, further efforts are needed in these and other areas, such as energy and transport. our credibility will suffer if unsustainable trends persist or if our policies have detrimental impacts outside the eu, in particular on the development opportunities of the poorest countries. on sustainable consumption and production, the eu has been playing a leading role by promoting a broad mix of policies and tools, such as integrated pollution prevention and control, the eco-management and audit scheme and eco-labelling, as well as sectoral instruments in key areas such as energy or agriculture. but we should not try to reinvent the wheel: we are assessing the measures and instruments implemented so far and identifying gaps. we are also working with member states to provide an overall assessment by the end of 2003. poverty eradication has been, and will continue to be, at the centre of our world summit commitments, as will the development dimension. this is a key issue when working towards the achievement of all internationally agreed development goals. on the issue of financing for development, the commission has been asked by member states to closely monitor the commitments made before the monterrey conference. continued efforts will be needed to stick to our commitments against a background of sluggish economic growth and fiscal austerity. in concluding, let me welcome parliament's support in pushing for the eu to be in the forefront when it comes to delivery. two weeks ago the european commission adopted a communication on our cooperation with the united nations. it was entitled: 'the choice of multilateralism' and in it we stated that the eu should adopt a determined front-runner approach to the negotiation and implementation of important initiatives in the fields of sustainable development, poverty reduction and international security. we also called upon the un itself to follow more closely an approach based on benchmarking and clear targets in the follow-up to major conferences, such as the world summit. i am confident that i can count on parliament's continued support in pursuing these efforts.

do not think, however, that this initiative goes far enough. where a merger has clear crossborder effects, it should be dealt with by the commission as far as possible. referral to the commission should be possible on the basis of objective criteria and at the request of the merging parties. we have drawn up specific proposals to that end. for the same reasons, caution is warranted in referring mergers to member states. concentrations which meet the requirements of a simplified procedure should not, in principle, be referred to the member states. one of the objectives of the revision of the regulation is to strengthen legal certainty. the commission's proposal to extend the concept of economic dominance - to extend the definition - leads, in our view, to the opposite. any merger which gives rise to a competitive advantage will fall within the new definition. the practice has been adapted to the present definition, which has been the subject of extensive case law. changing the definition creates uncertainty and unnecessary legal uncertainty. in addition, we believe that there is a danger of the market being robbed of its dynamism if the concentration process is intervened on a much larger scale than is currently the case. i therefore advocate that the definition be left unchanged. we agree to leave article 2 (1) unchanged: however, the requirements for demonstrating efficiencies should not be overly stringent. it is a question of future benefits and it is impossible to give a 100 per cent guarantee that those benefits will indeed occur. there is a need for greater clarity on the timing of the provision of relevant information on efficiencies. the commission recommends the following: substantially extend its investigative powers. this is in accordance with regulation no 1 of 2003 on cartel procedures. however, we believe that there is a fundamental difference between the objective of merger control and the objective of combating cartel infringements. in contrast to cartel offences, a merger investigation does not involve the assumption of wrongdoing. we consider the commission's proposal to increase the resources for research in this regulation to be excessive, especially when viewed in the light of the enormous fines that the commission may impose for non-compliance with the regulation. no one can be forced to incriminate himself, which is an important principle of criminal law and should apply here as well. it is therefore not a luxury to reiterate in the regulation that the commission must respect the rights of the persons concerned in the context of an investigation. this applies in particular to the right of silence of the company lawyer, which should also apply to the other employees who are subject to questioning by the commission. i would also like to point out once again the lack of internal and external controls on the commission's decision-making. in the present situation, the investigating and decision-making authorities are still not separated. i find that difficult to reconcile with the demand for legal certainty and independence. the legitimacy of decision-making will be further enhanced by the establishment of a specialised competition chamber at the court of first instance. this would also help speed up the procedure and improve the quality of justice.

mr president, rail transport was once started by private companies hoping to make a profit from it. their railway lines did not form a coherent network and were often not accessible to trains of other companies with different characteristics. many of these companies went bankrupt or were noted for their poor quality and frequently interrupted service. when that system failed, state-owned enterprises came along, trying to develop as much of a unified model for their country as possible. rail transport became a core task of the state. we have now reached a stage where, on the one hand, a large-scale european unity model is being pursued, but on the other hand, a return to the 19th century model of individual private enterprises is being promoted. these two objectives are likely to prove incompatible in practice and to lead to continuing tensions. the proponents of this model place highly developed transport companies in a free market, such as airlines and truck companies, for example, on the railways, which are considered old-fashioned. free competition would lead to growth and attractiveness for a wider customer base that has not used the railway until now. others fear that liberalisation will only lead to a separation between profitable and loss-making activities and to cuts in infrastructure, services and staff, with less security and higher fares as a result. instead of creating space for new private companies, there would be more reason to put long distance cross-border transport in the hands of a good coordination between existing national companies or in the hands of one single european company. measures to reduce environmentally unfriendly air and road transport would be a good complement to this. the four reports before us today are the product of this important disagreement. the common feature is that they also provide for the future of rail transport, and this is progress compared with the time when the railway was referred to the museum for 19th century rarities. but there are sharp differences of opinion on how to achieve this. the jarzembowski report is part of an endless series of attempts to liberalize more and faster, not only for cross-border goods transport but even for domestic passenger transport. although i am not in favour of the council having too much power, i hope that if the majority of this parliament follows the rapporteur, the council will again limit and curb these attempts. the sterckx report puts less emphasis on a free market, but is rather centralistic in its thinking, leaving little room for national and regional measures. the ainardi and savary reports are aimed at quality for society, users and staff and therefore have my support.
these proposals, mr president, are intended to give a boost to the railway sector so that it can become an attractive and viable alternative to other modes of transport. the white paper has been widely welcomed. the question is how to do it. a major change of mentality is needed within the sector. this package can certainly contribute to this, provided it is properly developed and implemented. one important element is market access. who gets rights of use - and for what? in order to cope with competition from road transport, a similar freedom for carriers and shippers is necessary. direct access to the rail network for freight transport stakeholders. i doubt whether it will make sense in the short term to extend this to passenger transport. when we give entrepreneurs this space, it is important that we set clear rules for use and safety. we believe that mr sterckx has put his finger in the right places. we can therefore agree with most of his proposals. that is also true of a number of proposals in mr ainardi's report. with regard to the functioning of the agency: the development of the railways in recent decades has not brought us what we had hoped for. the agency will therefore have to provide an incentive to move in a new direction. we shall have to take this into account when we consider the participation of the various parties concerned. i would like to say that i am very pleased that the commission has taken this initiative.

guidelines we adopted at the beginning of this year. what have been the main issues for parliament so far? we want to make the integration of the new countries into the european union a success. the enlargement must be a success and that is why we have said from the beginning: the 25 countries must be represented in a single budget. secondly, we said: we want to do something to stimulate economic enterprises in the new member states, as well as in the old ones. the third point is: we must make it as easy as possible for the new member states to integrate into the old ones. this budget for 2004 - as has been said several times in previous debates - has a number of special features. we will now present a budget for 25 countries, but we all know that we will not have a european union of 25 member states until 1 may next year. that is why we shall vote in december on a budget for 15 countries, with a technical annex for the 10 new countries. we shall then vote on a supplementary budget for these 10 new countries in the course of next year. another new feature of the 2004 budget is activity-based budgeting. we have discovered some imperfections in it. we hope that this can be rectified in the course of the year. what is most important for parliament is that we can check the extent to which the programmes are being implemented and what types of evaluation techniques are available. we have voted for a budget of austerity in general. the payment appropriations have been increased, as have other payment appropriations, but overall i think we can achieve this result, even at a time when all of europe is cutting back. i would like to say a few words about the various chapters of the budget. firstly, the agricultural budget, chapter 1. we are waiting for the amendment, which will be published shortly. we hope that the initiatives of parliament, which have been reaffirmed in this budget and which were also mentioned in previous resolutions, namely the pilot projects or preparatory actions concerning the environmental indicators, the animal diseases fund, the development of better vaccines and the development of a quality policy for agricultural products, will also be reflected in the commission's note of amendments which will be published shortly. we will no doubt also learn what effect the more expensive euro has had on agricultural policy. we have also voted in the committee on budgets on a number of other points: we want more research into animal welfare and we want, among other things, more alternatives to tobacco growing in europe. as regards chapter 2, the structural funds. we have increased the payment appropriations in comparison with what the council considered reasonable. we did that for two reasons. firstly, the member states themselves think they can spend much more than the commission proposes each year. we have tried to please the member states. secondly, we are concerned about the slow implementation of structural policy. we believe that we can improve this by increasing payment appropriations. you will say: "is it appropriate to increase payment credits at this time?" if we look at the increase in payment appropriations in the previous years, i think it is a very modest increase compared to those previous years. as regards chapter 3, the internal policies. we believe that the most important initiative is to encourage small and mediumsized enterprises in the new member states. that can be done with relatively little money. with an amount of 33 million more than in the council budget, and with a corresponding multiplier effect of 20 to 30, we can give the small and mediumsized enterprises in eastern europe much more guarantees so that these enterprises can develop. at the same time we will be introducing a training programme for bank managers. the chapter on internal policies gives an additional increase to the council for measures to be taken in connection with the still increasing pollution of the sea. we know the european maritime agency, which certainly has its work to do, but we felt we had to limit the appropriations proposed by the commission because there is no legal basis yet. we hope that it will be in the course of this year. we have also paid a great deal of attention to the agencies this year. more and more agencies are coming. there's more on the way. we want better parliamentary control over these agencies. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval. we also want to pay more attention to the organigram of the agencies, just as we are interested in the organigram for the commission itself. these are not difficult requirements for the agencies. we hope that we can find a solution to this before the second reading. a few other points need to be made in connection with chapter 3. we believe that the council should decide as soon as possible on the seat of the agencies. it's a great uncertainty as long as this hasn't happened. we believe that vat fraud should be further investigated. the info points are a matter of great concern to parliament. the new financial regulation means that some of these info difficulties of eurostat. we have put 25% of the money for eurostat in reserve pending the final report, which we expect by the end of october. there was also a lot of discussion about chapter 4: the european union is not a political entity. the situation in iraq is predominant in all of this. we think that something needs to be done in iraq. we have included in the budget a provision of 30 million and we are aware that the commission has made a proposal for 200 million, of which 40 million will probably be paid from the 2003 budget and 160 million from the 2004 budget, perhaps using the resolutions and in the resolution of parliament itself. i'll give you a few examples: the commission must be able to take account of the fact that the number of vacancies in the commission is less ineffectiveness of structural fund policies. in summary, the researchers conclude that structural fund policy can only be effective if the following four conditions are met. firstly, the quality of the institutions. secondly, low inflation. thirdly, a transparent and reliable public policy. fourth, the level of corruption is low. it is a pity that the four largest recipients of structural fund president. - the next item is the report (a4-0173/97) by mr de gucht, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection, on the proposal from the commission to the council (com (97) 0173 - c4-0173/97) for a directive amending directive 76/769/eec on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to cosmetic products (rapporteur: mr de gucht) in the future, for example, cell transplantation will play an increasingly important role in mainstream medicine. consider the transplantation of adult stem cells, for example. however, there are two aspects which must be regulated by the european union in this context. firstly, the quality and safety of donation and transplantation. secondly, the prevention of trafficking in organs, tissues and cells. the first point is currently being dealt with in the liese report and the second point in the report we are discussing today. in short, we can wholeheartedly support this report. it is good that these immoral practices are being addressed. it is good that the report calls for extra attention to encourage voluntary donation. there is one point in the report that we cannot follow: we believe that, as the greek initiative states, the offering and accepting of money for organs, tissues or cells should also be punishable.
mr president, commissioner, in order to prevent cod from disappearing completely from the north sea, a 'save the cod' action is urgently needed. the question is: - what? in its final cod recovery plan, the commission introduces a system of fishing effort limitation. this system has long proved its worth in the netherlands as the 'seed days' scheme, a scheme which allows fishing pressure to be well controlled. yet the plan also has its inevitable hooks and eyes. it only concerns vessels longer than 10 metres, whereas shorter vessels do have a share in the cod catch. the same applies to sport fishing. in fact, industrial fishing, which regularly catches large quantities of cod, is almost untouched. the proportionality of the measures to be taken is unclear. fishermen who catch little cod by-catch should be less hampered in their activities by the recovery plan than fishermen who contribute relatively more to the problems. the effects of the different fisheries can only be properly measured if the discards are also landed. a proposal to that effect is lacking.
mr president, i should like to begin by congratulating the rapporteur, mrs stihler, on her report. and i hope that her next marathon, which will be in new york, i thought, will be as successful as this report. then the cod fishery will be fine. mr president, the problem of cod stocks is well known. it's just that our approach to the problem is constantly changing. on the one hand, ices is now suggesting that we should stop all catches, and at the same time, canadian biologists are saying that it doesn't make sense, that it won't lead to the recovery of the cod stock. this means that the problem is difficult and can only be solved if there is genuine cooperation between the commission, the regions and the fisheries sector. it is extremely important that the efforts and commitment of fishermen be involved in this. the only way to tackle these problems is to give a stronger position to producer groups of fishermen. joint management of quotas, joint efforts to reduce by-catches as much as possible and joint consideration of how to deal with the consequences of a reduction in catches. the commission should be generous in its use of the structural funds for the regions which are most affected by the reduction in cod catches. perhaps these resources could be used to attract other jobs to these regions. i would like to reiterate my support for mr stihler's approach and i hope that the commission will take this report very seriously.

now, the eu has been trying to reduce the capacity of the fleet of european fishermen. but this reduction has not been achieved in practice. the problems of overfishing in europe are being felt in the the rapporteur. in some countries, it is sometimes forgotten that the european parliament is a co-legislator. the current ala regulation was adopted ten years ago as a regulation for the asian and latin american regions. the european parliament has since called for two separate regulations for two such different regions. the european commission has, however, again put forward a proposal to modernise the existing regulation and at the same time to incorporate the regulation on aid to uprooted people, which is due to expire at the end of next year. as if that parliamentary resolution had never existed! the committee on development and cooperation therefore proposes to split the regulation into two separate regulations by means of amendments. as rapporteur, i attach great importance to presenting this message from the committee on development and cooperation to you. of course, this will still require extensive consultation with the council. but the distinction to be made will be clear to all. now, to the content. the commission wants a 'light legal framework' for its development cooperation activities in both regions. it's become a very light frame. the main objective of development cooperation is the fight against and ultimate eradication of poverty, as also expressed in the millennium development goals. i do not find this clearly reflected in the commission's proposal. other objectives, such as education, health, the environment and democratization, are also lacking. and that is why i have put forward, as a first point, that 35% of expenditure should be devoted to social infrastructure, as we have regularly included in the budget since 2001. of this, at least 20 percent should be spent on basic health care and basic education, because so far these millennium development goals have been very poorly met. secondly, education in particular is a very important tool in the fight against poverty. everyone has the right to and should have access to all forms of education, regardless of their origin, gender or age. a disproportionate share of the poor in developing countries are women, but they are the ones who are often denied this right. they are the carriers of water. i therefore strongly advocate gender mainstreaming and even more attention to women and girls, not only in education and health care, but also in social, economic and above all political life. they should be able to participate as full members in the functioning of society. another important point is the question of collusion. the non-negotiations of the wto in cancún have once again clearly underlined the need for full participation by the developing countries. this is true not only at governmental level but also in the lower regions. it is therefore crucial that all stakeholders are consulted when preparing the strategy papers, the annual indicative programmes and the annual action plans for development cooperation. not only the government bodies at national, regional and local level, but also the parliamentarians in those countries, the ngos, the private sector and all other relevant actors of civil society. they know their own needs better than anyone else and can therefore clearly indicate what is needed. this is also a great wish that has come to us from the field. only in this way can a form of ownership of the various policies and actions in development cooperation be realised for all sections of the population. it is important that the european parliament, as a co-legislator, should also be involved and remain involved in european development policy. the commission is therefore expected to submit the above strategy papers to parliament as well. it seems to me to be self-evident that it should not only describe the sectoral and inter-sectoral priorities and specific objectives, but also the expected results on the basis of appropriate performance indicators. as a dutchman and a liberal, i attach great importance to the useful and effective use of taxpayers' money. and this can only be tested by setting clear objectives and performance indicators. finally, i would like to emphasize once again that the european mr president, is the european union going to finance research involving human embryos, yes or no? that is the central question. the great importance of this subject lies in this: the debate on funding is really a debate on ethics. a discussion of right and wrong. not that . whether the funding is adequate or not, but: is this research good in itself or not? that's what this is really about. when we discuss the financing of stem cell research, why can we not simply say that in many member states this research is not allowed and that we should not therefore allocate common funds to it? what's wrong with that line of reasoning? if it were not done in some member states, okay. but it is a criminal offence in a number of member states. how can we ask member states to contribute to research that is fundamentally opposed? that's a slap in the face to those union boys, isn't it? i'm all for stem cell research. i believe it is our duty to seek therapies for diseases that are now considered incurable. i am also in favour of the eu providing financial resources for this. but, and this is where i think ethics comes into play, this research cannot be done at the expense of other human lives. human life, at whatever stage of development, must never be used merely as an instrument! mr president, shipping and ports are more prone to abuse than many other businesses. it concerns the treatment of crossborder flows of goods between different states, not only within the european union but throughout the world. these countries differ not only in legislation but also in pay, working conditions, safety and environmental protection. such differences are a welcome tool for those who see social dumping and environmental pollution as a means of winning a competition. the phenomenon of the 'cheap flags' has existed for many years in maritime shipping, where ships owned by european shipowners are registered in a third world country. then they pay low taxes, they don't have to follow a lot of rules, and they can hire a crew with third-world salaries. companies owned by eu residents compete with each other through the international jungle. the fact that this jungle has been kept as far away from the door as possible in european ports has not come about by itself. without the long struggle of the trade unions and the municipal port companies, there would have been cheap ports, internationally known as ports of convenience, long ago. ports with a declining level of remuneration, safety and environmental protection. ports where only temporary work exists, which is dirty and unsafe and attracts mainly unskilled labour. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's fishing fleet is not disrupted. in such a competition, ports serving a common hinterland will destroy each other. the winner will always be the most antisocial, the most environmentally unfriendly, the most unsafe and therefore the cheapest port. if the european union is to harmonize port rules, they must aim to eliminate unfair and dangerous competition by group of ports with a common hinterland. this problem is particularly acute in the ports around the north sea, from dunkirk in france via the belgian and dutch ports to hamburg in germany. railways, rivers, and canals connect these ports with much of the same industrial area and with cities full of consumers. for a long time, these ports, with their large public investments, low tariffs and great secrecy, have tried to squeeze customers away from each other. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. a port directive, which provides the best level of protection for registered and qualified port workers throughout europe and prevents accidents to ships as a result of loading errors, as happened in february with the danish cargo ship karin cat. such a port directive would be in line with a number of recent environmental measures taken by the european union, which aim to make it more difficult to dump ship waste and cargo residues at sea and to prevent single-hull tankers from leaving european ports in the long term. instead, the european commission has proposed a directive that does the opposite. by making existing protection of registered port workers against unfair competition at member state level more difficult or weaker, that competition will only increase. this may reduce the cost of handling goods at port, but in most cases it was already a negligible part of the cost of production. both at first reading two years ago and at second reading in march this parliament corrected those plans. although the correction was less far-reaching than the unions had requested and left loopholes open for abuse, the parties involved with different interests seemed to be able to live reasonably with it. that is no longer the case since the council of transport ministers systematically refused to adopt those improvements last summer. in the conciliation procedure, the parliament's delegation initially seemed determined to continue along the line previously adopted by parliament. that was not just the case with the left-wing groups, but i heard it from christian democrats and liberals as well. on 29 september, these objections were suddenly largely accepted. in exchange for a more detailed study of competition and a text that plays with the words 'may' and 'must', eight of the 15 members gave up the achievements set by parliament. the fact that a directive was being drawn up was suddenly more important than its precise content. the final proposal closely resembles spanish and italian laws for monopoly ports with a small hinterland around the mediterranean. application to other parts of europe will lead to more labour disputes and abuses, especially in the north sea ports. the commission has already made it clear on several occasions that it will not accept this. in these circumstances, the directive is counterproductive and should not be introduced. this proposal deserves to be rejected on thursday. mr president, there is a big difference between the word 'must' and the word 'may'. the current directive, which is now before the council following conciliation, allows ports to introduce a licensing system, particularly for loading and unloading themselves. the jarzembowski report, which we adopted earlier at second reading, also said that ports should introduce a licensing system. the compromise text differs in a significant respect from the text as adopted at second reading. the difference between 'may' and 'must' has major implications for ports and port workers in europe. a non-compulsory licensing system encourages unfair competition, which can be detrimental to the quality of employment in ports that have a good licensing system. that can never have been the intention of this liberalization. secondary ports will remain and the unfair competition that results may affect the quality of employment in well-organised ports. for the labour party, my party, there has always been one point at the forefront and that is our minimum. self-loading and unloading must be well regulated through a good licensing system, which applies to everyone. in the conciliation procedure, this was given away. there will now be no compulsory licensing system for self-handling. in short, there is no real harmonisation in a core business such as self-loading and unloading, which allows different regimes to be used in different ports. it has thus become a false example of liberalisation. it is strange that in many situations the eu is able to impose detailed rules on mr jan en alleman, but in this case, when it comes to the quality of jobs, it is not able to do so. we can explain that to the people whose interests are at stake here. it will therefore not surprise anyone, after hearing me, that my group has no choice but to vote against this directive.

commission. – mr president, i wish to begin by thanking the european parliament, the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy and, in particular, the rapporteur, mr blokland, for the work they have put into the first reading report. our proposal aims to ensure consistency in dealing with shipments of waste. we need to ensure environmentally sound management in relation to both shipments within the community and exports from the community to third countries. it is focused on implementing the 2001 oecd decision, pursuing international harmonisation, which means respecting the internationally agreed obligations in the basel convention, addressing problems encountered in the application of the regulation since its adoption ten years ago and enhancing the structure of the regulation. in relation to shipments within the community, i share the concerns expressed about standard dumping in waste for recovery. the commission proposal and the communication on a thematic strategy on the prevention and recycling of waste clearly recognise the problem. however, our response is a long-term solution at eu level, whose main elements are, firstly, the establishment of standards at eu level through the extension of the ippc directive and, secondly, the establishment of guidelines regarding sham or fake recovery and clearer distinctions between the different recovery and disposal operations. in relation to exports from the community to third countries, i support the amendments adopted by the committee on the environment to further sharpen the regulation by making reference to both eu legislation and certain internationally-agreed guidelines, in particular those on ship recycling. let me conclude this introduction by saying that it is important that we do not allow environmental standard dumping, either when we ship waste internally within the community or when we export it from the community to third countries.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the waste is disposed of in a safe manner. the reason for this is that there are different market conditions. not all member states have landfill bans or charges. this is what makes a lot of waste go to other countries. this is contrary to the principles of proximity and self-care, which apply to the disposal of waste under the waste framework directive. waste shipments can only be refused if the waste is not being put to good use in the importing country. much debate has arisen as to when something can be considered a useful application. the problem with this whole discussion is that the useful use of waste does not mean that it is better for the environment. it is therefore necessary to develop clear criteria for useful application. the european commission recognises this problem, noting, among other things, that few environmental requirements are imposed on operations which lead to useful use. however, there is no prospect of a solution to this problem at present, except that the commission will come forward with proposals in the context of the thematic strategy for recycling. at the moment the court of justice is deciding what is the useful use of waste and this is not acceptable. the amendment of the waste framework directive has also been delayed for too long. it is not responsible to the waste sector to wait for the whole lengthy process of adapting the framework directive on waste. there is a need for clarity in the short term. since the problems arise mainly in the shipment of waste, it is obvious that these additional conditions should be formulated in a very specific way in this regulation. the environment committee believes that as long as these conditions are not formulated by the european commission, member states should be able to impose conditions on the recovery of waste themselves. i also believe that it should be possible to refuse shipments of waste if a minimum percentage of useful use and a minimum caloric value are not met. there is still a misunderstanding about these grounds for refusal. the possibility of refusing a waste shipment on environmental grounds does not imply an obligation to refuse. some of the position papers wrongly state that waste shipments are prohibited. articles 12 and 13 of this regulation do not refer to a prohibition but to the fact that a shipment of waste can take place by mutual consent. so silver recycling, even if it is less than one tenth of a percent, is still possible. export of waste should only be allowed if it leads to recovery or final disposal in the short term. so, as far as the environment committee is concerned: no waste exports intended for so-called provisional recovery or temporary disposal. in practice, this mixing, sorting and storing goes very wrong. there is no way of knowing where the waste has gone or what has happened to it. waste that is properly sorted, well defined and actually used or disposed of in an environmentally sound manner can therefore be exported. the commission is also proposing a ban on the export of unsorted household waste. we do not transfer our waste water to another country. a final point concerns the implementation of this regulation. we must not give in to member states who are not investing enough in this. i therefore oppose amendments nos 95 and 98 by the european people's party which introduce tacit authorization for the importing country. the transparency requires prior written consent of both parties. there are member states whose affairs are not in order at the moment. they themselves admit that they cannot control the waste shipments. the member states concerned should change this rather than complaining about administrative burdens. in conclusion, mr president, on the european waste market price competition is acceptable, but environmental competition is not. what the environment committee does not want is waste exports which lead to an environmentally less hygienic alternative. the aim of this regulation is not to facilitate trade in waste but to enable waste management to be carried out in an environmentally sound manner.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to congratulate mr blokland on a good and clear report. environmental dumping is still a major problem after 28 years. this is partly because environmental standards are not the same everywhere, especially because there is a great deal of controversy about what is actually useful application. there are no clear criteria. the european commission has made some very bad mistakes in this area. it should have taken the initiative to clarify this matter many years ago. but unfortunately the commission has bowed to the pressure of the waste industry, which prefers to continue dumping waste. the european court of justice in luxembourg has now made some rulings in this legal vacuum, but they do not give a final answer to the question of what exactly is useful application. in my group, burning everything is not a useful application. unfortunately, that is now the case by definition. burning newspapers is not useful, recycling paper is much more useful. of course, after five to seven times of recycling paper, you can't recycle any more, and then burning might be useful. the burning of sewage sludge is also considered useful by definition. but the question is whether that is wise. if the sludge is leaking, it may be useful, but it's certainly not full of water. we must now have this political debate and the committee on the environment has done that. we shall also be voting on amendments tomorrow. since the commission has not provided any clarification, we must do so. it is not worth waiting for a thematic strategy and then thinking about legislation. that's five years away. we're gonna have to try to fill this hole as best and as bad as we can.
commission. – mr president, i thank the european parliament and, in particular, mrs gutiérrez-cortines, for the preparation of this report. with this, the consultation process on the first phase of the soil thematic strategy will be concluded. the commission welcomes parliament's broad support for the general approach, main objectives and deliverables presented in the communication. this includes the development of a communication on major soil degradation issues such as erosion, contamination and organic matter, as well as a proposal for a soil monitoring directive. the european parliament recognises the community dimension for many of the soil degradation processes europe is faced with. parliament underlines that soil degradation processes are progressive and often go unnoticed, sometimes for many decades. this distinguishes soil from other environmental components and goes some way towards explaining why air and water policies were developed earlier. the commission shares the view that any approach to soil protection must take account of the considerable diversity of regional and local conditions that exist across europe. the european strategy for soil protection does not mean a standardised, one-size-fits-all approach. the commission fully agrees that it is vital to apply an integrated approach to soil, based on sustainable development. the multifunctional and cross-sectoral approach to soil is of primary importance. the economic and social implications of soil degradation are therefore an integral part of the soil thematic strategy. the numerous detailed comments, requests and additional proposals contained in parliament's resolution will be fully taken into account in the future development of the soil thematic strategy. in this context the commission welcomes parliament's support for the knowledge-based approach. the commission will examine the detailed proposals for a soil catalogue, soil mapping and zoning, which should be geared to solving specific soil degradation problems. we also recognise that it is necessary to gain greater understanding of soil biodiversity, the nutrient and water cycles and the issues related to the use of compost. the commission welcomes the important role attributed to agriculture and forestry in revitalising soil – in particular, the call to make cross-compliance compulsory for all payments under the common agricultural policy; the integration of specific measures for soil and water protection into the cap; the localised diagnosis of the impacts of cap reform on soil health; and the definition of patterns of agriculture and forestry, in line with soil characteristics. the commission welcomes parliament's request to bring land use into line with soil characteristics, to integrate soil protection objectives into spatial planning strategies, to prevent the indiscriminate sealing of land and to prevent the bisection of ecosystems, waterflows and landscapes by road and urban infrastructures. the commission recognises the need to develop more leadership in europe in the area of spatial planning. the commission fully subscribes to the role attributed to soil protection in the context of major processes such as biodiversity decline, climate change, desertification, coastal erosion and forest fires. the commission recognises, in particular, the need for additional action to combat desertification in europe and will consider parliament's urgent call for an immediate communication and community action programme on desertification. in conclusion i would like to underline that i consider parliament's resolution as an important input to our work. we can now further direct our work on the development of the next stage on the soil strategy.
the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism has adopted a number of amendments to the proposal. president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, as humans we are very dependent on water and air, but also on the soil. we live on it and from it, we travel over it and its beauty fills us with wonder. reason enough to be careful with the soil. i would like to draw attention to some aspects of this care on behalf of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism. firstly, it is worth noting that the soil has fewer international aspects than air and water, which move. although the member states have similar soil problems to a certain extent, the causes of these problems are different. in this context, it is to be feared that a centralised approach for all member states will not produce the desired result. the emphasis of a european approach must therefore be on the exchange of information, knowledge and best practice. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. secondly, mrs gutiérrez rightly points to the negative effects of transport on the soil. soil cover and compaction are important negative effects of infrastructure on the soil, affecting the viability and condition of the same soil. it is therefore necessary to minimise these effects and thus reduce the burden on the soil. opportunities for this lie in promoting modes of transport with no or minimal impact on the ground such as inland and coastal shipping. but the use of less burdensome materials in the construction of infrastructure is also one of the possibilities. finally, the community will also have to exert its influence directly on the construction of infrastructure by including the land interest in projects in which the community invests. mr
