protection of soil is shaped.
the convention was established because the heads of government themselves have failed to make the union more democratic, more transparent and more efficient. the national governments have participated in the public discussions in the convention and signed the final outcome. but now, safe behind the closed doors of the igc, they feel free again to break the record open. the aim of the amendment is to change the annual budgetary procedure so that the lowest amount automatically counts for budget lines on which no agreement has been reached between the council and parliament. the dutch government defends this by saying that this makes the council and parliament equal, because whoever proposes the lowest amount will be the one who gets the money. at the same time, the dutch government is brazenly claiming that it is fighting for the full budgetary rights of parliament. now, there are two possibilities. either the ministers do not understand the consequences of what they are proposing and are not so clever, or they are trying to create so much confusion that they do not have to answer publicly for destroying the almost thirty-year-old democratic right of parliament to reject the budget. then they're just playing a trick. another difficult point is the financial perspective for the multiannual budget. they have been in existence since 1988, but in the form of interinstitutional agreements. parliament can always break such an agreement and thus has an important instrument of power in its hands. the financial perspective is now incorporated in the treaty. away with the power tool! what is worse is that some governments, following the example of the economic and financial affairs council, want the european parliament to have only an advisory role in the adoption of the multiannual budget, whereas we are now equal partners. the genuine attempt by the finance ministers to bring about a coup d'état threatens to harm not only parliament but also the ministers themselves. i think it is bizarre that the national ministers still do not understand this. let me give you an example. if the european parliament and the ministers for culture agree on a european multiannual cultural programme, the ministers for finance can eventually scrap it by simply proposing a lower amount in the annual budgetary procedure and demanding that the legislation be adapted to the budget rather than the other way around. who is in charge of europe now? the european parliament's acquired legislative power can become an empty shell when it has little power to ensure that sufficient money is available for the implementation of laws. the heads of government are threatening to replace 30 years of budgetary law with the all-powerful finance ministers behind closed doors, and there is little democracy or transparency in that. the rapporteur. president, commissioner, europe must do better for its citizens. that means achieving more results for crossborder problems in a more democratic way. our european house needs to be put in order. the citizens are looking at the house with a certain scepticism. we have had the convention for the last year and it has given us a constitution, at least in draft form. that in itself is very good news for the citizens and for europe. we've been over this before. but there are other methods of putting the european house in order. the report i am presenting to you tonight on behalf of our committee also deals with better, more democratic and more transparent governance. we can also carry out substantial reforms without changing the european treaties. improving european governance is one of the main strategic objectives of the prodi commission for the period 2000-04. in 2001 we came out with the white paper on european governance and as parliament we gave our opinion then and now two years later we are doing so again on the progress of the same white paper. some important progress has been made. for example, in april 2002 the commission started to simplify legislation. the legislation was reduced by as much as 35 000 pages. a major contribution to the simplification of european governance. the commission also published plans for consulting regional and local authorities, civil society organisations and experts. i would like to return to some of these points, but for all of them it is now a question of implementation. not just lip service, but action! the commission can do much more to bring europe closer to the citizen. i have made several proposals in this report. first and foremost: i believe that all legislative proposals should be subject to a so-called citizen test. this means that every time the commission makes a law, it must take account of the consequences of this on the daily life of the citizens for whom it is made. the economic, social and environmental consequences. that is the only way to ensure that we get off our ivory tower and no longer make laws in the air or from above. i call on my colleagues and the commission to support this initiative! i would also like to emphasize the fact that the european commission has deployed experts at an early stage of the legislative process. first of all, i have to say that experts are extremely helpful. secondly, i must say that there is a huge forest and a proliferation of expert groups, both permanent and ad hoc. 850 expert groups and over 500 sub-groups. it is not clear to anyone, not even to the commission, who exactly is involved. parliament has already called for the commission to publish clear lists of experts to be consulted on specific subjects. this gives parliament and the council, and i think even the commission, a clear picture of who is actually looking at those legislative proposals and an insight into the fundamental policy choices made during the policy-making process. if those lists are made available, it will help us all. i call on the commission to put this into practice now - after three years of promises - because we want a parliamentary democracy and not a democracy of experts. another important point i have mentioned is global governance. multilateralism and a broad concept of security, including peace and security, but also poverty reduction and sustainable development, have always been at the heart of foreign policy. it is time for the european union, the union's largest economic power, to commit itself to promoting its values on a global scale in the reform of multilateral institutions. but to do that we will require one vote from the eu. that could start in the security council with one seat. finally, the consultation of organisations. i have particularly stressed the need to consult local and regional authorities. "europe starts in the region". the regions are where the policies are to be implemented and where much of europe's funds are spent. the regions are also the places where citizens identify with themselves, sometimes even more than their own capitals, especially when regions cross borders. it is therefore important that the regional authorities have their own voice and that it be given to them in the legislative process. the commission has understood this and is prepared to make use of it. now, the practice, please. mr maccormick has made a very important report on this subject on the tripartite agreements. these contracts with member states and regional authorities can be a very useful instrument, because they will start to bring europe closer to the region and to give it real shape. it is a way of making european governance more efficient and closer to the citizen, and we wholeheartedly support the main lines of mr maccormick's report. finally, i would like to stress that it is the responsibility of all the institutions to achieve a credible, transparent and democratic administration. it is not just the commission's responsibility, but the responsibility of all the institutions. in this report we therefore call for an interinstitutional agreement on consultation to which all the institutions are bound. the reforms under the white paper on governance are of great importance for europe and its citizens. it's important that we take a firm stand now! and i thank you for giving me a little more speaking time than i was originally allocated.

in writing. - (nl) european rules prescribe the goods and services on which member states may impose high vat rates and those which, by way of derogation, may be subject to the reduced rate. this exception already applied to food and clothing, but in 1999 labour-intensive services were also introduced on an experimental basis into the category of goods subject to a reduced rate of vat. this has had a positive impact on employment. according to a recent hearing here in parliament, the deployment of this instrument has created an additional 250 000 jobs in the european union. there are other positive effects. if bicycle repair remains affordable, it will encourage cycling. it is astonishing that the commission now wants to put an end to this. the commission bases its decision on insufficient and incomplete investigations and does not have sufficient evidence to prove that the experiment has produced unsatisfactory results. if the experiment is stopped, countless jobs will disappear in europe, including 8 500 in the netherlands. my party, the dutch socialist party, sees taxes as a useful instrument for achieving sound social security and providing public services, but it denounces this way of applying tax increases. we want to keep the reduced vat rates for hairdressers, bicycle repairers and shoemakers. i would ask that the right of member states to maintain reduced vat rates for labour-intensive services be applied if this is supported by sound arguments from a social and employment point of view.

in writing. - the eppl is disappointed that further amendments to strengthen the information and consultation provisions of the directive were narrowly rejected by a coalition led by the epp and the liberals. the eplp supported amendments which gave employees more information and consultation rights during the tendering process. however, we agree that this directive represents an improvement on the july 2001 directive in terms of information and consultation of employees. articles 6, 9 and 13 improve the rights of employees. the commission's initial proposal provided that the provisions of the information and consultation directive would not prejudice the public tender directive. it is now clear that the directive on public tenders is also without prejudice to the directive on information and consultation. the eplp considers that this is a matter of political judgment: is it better to have no directive and therefore allow the maintenance of an unregulated market in takeover bids, with no information or transparency on company structures and little or no guarantee of employees' rights to information and consultation, or is it better to vote for a directive that allows substantial progress in creating an open and transparent framework for takeover bids, with the introduction of new standards guaranteeing both employees' and investors' rights? we voted for the second option.
in writing. - (pt) i took part in the conciliation committee meeting on 4 july 2001 on this subject, at which the agreement between parliament and the council was blocked. the aim was to require the boards of directors of the companies subject to a takeover bid to refrain from adopting defensive measures against the bidder or the bidding company. today, the european parliament is approving, in essence, a set of rules in this area. these rules provide that member states and companies will have the possibility - but not the obligation - to make unlawful defensive measures which have not been formally approved by general meetings of shareholders. this new wording, which is in line with the protection of minority shareholders in the event of a takeover bid and which marks the unlocking of this important area of company law and international economic and financial life, leads me to believe that this report deserves my support.

- mr president, my group is opposed to the lifting of the arms embargo and we therefore support the general line of not lifting the arms embargo against china now. i'd like to add a few things. anyone who has visited china on several occasions over the last 10 years - including myself - knows that there is a huge economic dynamism there, with great differences between the different regions and also with an almost rigid capitalism at the internal level, with many major social problems. in a society that evolves like this, you also need a political system that can handle this. there is clearly a huge tension between economic freedom, which leaves little room for social actors such as the trade union movement and others to shape it in the social sphere, and the political sphere, which leaves no room for political democracy. the whole process, of course, we all look at it with breathless eyes. china is not a small player. it's big and powerful in terms of economy, it's big and powerful in terms of population. so if you're trying to look at that region from a geopolitical standpoint, don't just look at it in relation to taiwan. of course, that's one point, but it's much wider in that region. china, of course, is gradually becoming a global player. china is trying to launch a charm offensive. they are well aware that their enormous economic power is also a source of fear for many people and that they are trying to be a positive player on the global stage. to do so, they must effectively create more room for democracy and respect for human rights in their own countries. they are not yet managing that tension well, and some of them do not want to manage it at all or even do something that we think is impossible, namely freedom on the one hand and political unfreedom on the other. but we in europe have a great interest in helping them to take up this new role. so all my colleagues are right to say: no lifting of the arms embargo, that's the wrong signal. but at the same time, ladies and gentlemen, let us put this in a broader perspective and let us make it clear that we really want this in-depth dialogue with china - mr president, the death penalty is a terrible thing. it's a medieval phenomenon, used by governments that couldn't guard their prisoners and therefore killed them before they could escape. but in the present times it is even worse. the phenomenon of the "death penalty" will be at its worst when it is also used as a political tool by governments against oppositions. and the philippines has a history of incessant violence. and today, those problems are still unresolved. it is clear from the history of the last hundred years: the united states took over the spanish colonies in 1898, then a kind of self-determination in 1946, but then governments came to power that dealt with the population in a very dictatorial way, especially the long-term dictatorship of marcos. and since then, there have been only weak governments. president-elect changes, but with a powerful military in the background, without taking into account the opposition and certainly without taking into account the independence movements, movements which saw a future apart from the philippines or in a loose cooperation with the other parts of the philippines. and that is why there are constant forms of guerrilla warfare. in the philippines today, the left is allowed to have three members in the legislature, but in a sort of semi-illegal way, while other parts of the same left are considered terrorist organizations. under such circumstances, capital punishment is a deadly instrument in the hands of a government that does not want to hear any other voices and that stands in the way of any other solutions. whereas the present philippine governments, the successive governments, have never succeeded in solving the fundamental problems of poverty, deprivation, oppression and violence. and everything should be done from the outside and from the inside to give the philippines a peaceful and prosperous future, and that cannot be done with the instrument of the death penalty.
mr president, commissioner verheugen made some stirring remarks to moldova during his visit to chisinau on 5 december. he spoke of "european perspectives". verheugen also announced a special eu action plan for moldova by may 2004. i hope very much that it will be a practical support plan, which will not raise unrealistic expectations in chisinau. the international community has not yet been able to reach a consensus on the situation in the transnistrian republic. the political and military role of the russian federation is evident here. it is the litmus test for the near future whether the european union and russia are really pursuing common objectives of stability and security on our continent. talk about good neighborliness! transnistria, an urgent matter for the council and commission in their relations with the kremlin. speaking of eu priorities!
president. - the predominantly romanian-speaking area formerly known as bessarabia and now moldova was romanian between the two world wars, but was russian before and after. when the soviet union collapsed, the same national colors were chosen as those of the romanian flag, and many thought of returning. since then, the country has been torn by different views on its political future. in the two clashing populations, many follow an old-fashioned kind of authoritarian communists who seem best able to keep people alive despite low income levels. but that's the only thing they agree on. the slavic-speaking minority, especially in the narrow strip of land on the eastern bank of the dniester river, wants to maintain the traditionally strong ties with ukraine, russia and belarus. the romanian-speaking majority in the rest of the country would probably have joined romania long ago if it had not been so far behind in western europe. as romania is now, few feel the urgency of joining that much larger country. within romania too, the drive to win back moldova has become less urgent. in fact, during my visit to romania last year, i heard a romanian member of parliament proudly say that romania is the only country that is still strictly adhering to the molotov-ribbentrop pact, which established the new western borders of the soviet union on the eve of the second world war. the european union must be careful not to set itself up as the eternal guardian of that short-lived agreement between stalin and hitler. within moldova, the two warring populations have previously agreed to peacefully disintegrate in the event of majority accession to romania. we are therefore wise to take into account the possibility that the dniester river will in future again be the state border between romania and ukraine. we must not forget that variant either.
